17.       The Committee was informed that in the Tenth Plan CSIR has endeavoured to create major and innovative
 knowledge networks across and beyond CSIR laboratories.   In persuing this, some well focused programmes/projects were
 identified and formulated with a view to synergise the competencies developed in laboratories and get them implemented in
 a network mode.  The enhanced allocation of Rs. 163.59 crore (Rs. 130 crore Plan and Rs. 33.59 crore Non Plan) is
 essentially to provide appropriate support to the projects approved by the Planning Commission, in the last quarter of the
 previous financial year, under “National Laboratories” Scheme.  Further, the increase in the Non-plan allocation would help
 to meet partly, shortfall in grant for payment of research fellowship etc. It would also meet the increased pensionary
 requirement of CSIR pensioners.
18.       It was also informed that during the current year, under Technology Promotion, Development and Utilization
 (TPDU) Programmes it is proposed to provide support to: consortium projects for technology development; setting up of
 technology and innovation management centres, technology trade facilitation centres, consultancy clinics & design
 engineering centres; and development of IT based modern tools for optimum utilization of resources available in the
 country and promoting collaborative research among industries and institutions.
NATIONAL LABORATORIES      
19.       CSIR has a network of 38 Laboratories and 47 field stations/extension centres/regional centres located all over the
 country that undertake R&D in various S&T areas and disciplines.   The extension and regional centres have been
 established to reach the diverse users and disseminate knowledge and information of R&D capabilities, techniques and
 technologies developed by the National laboratories of CSIR.
 20.      Under the National Laboratories, three types of activities are carried out, namely:
·
                    Continually building and refurbishing competence at globally competitive level, skills and
 competency in all scientific areas;
·                    Taking up in-house projects with well defined objectives, deliverables, time frame; and
·                    Performing contract R&D for industry and other users to deal with problems through expertise gained
 over the years.
 
21.       A key feature of CSIR’s programmes during the Tenth Plan is the creation of major and innovative knowledge
 networks across and beyond CSIR laboratories.The focus of the programmes thus evolved have been to synergise the vast
 competence developed in CSIR Laboratories and to implement the programmes/projects in network mode.  The emphasis is
 also on deriving maximum output from less input.  Accordingly, categorisation of programmes under National Laboratories
 have been carried out keeping in view the requirement at the national level, at CSIR level and at the laboratory level.   Some
 of the projects would be implemented in a mission mode while others would be to further develop core competence.
 22.       In Tenth Five year Plan period, CSIR will undertake programmes that promote:
·
                    excellence in science-science that will lead and not follow;
·                    global competitiveness-technology based on high science rooted wherever feasible in India’s rich
 heritage of knowledge;
·                    local relevance-finding holistic and optimal solutions to the pressing problems of the people; and
·                    innovation in all spheres of activities ranging from science to technology management to financing.
 
23.       Projects of the Tenth Five Year Plan have been evolved over a period of one year, through interactive and repetitive
 consultations with the Steering Committee on S&T, Working Group for Tenth Five Year Plan, Sectoral Subgroup of the
 Working Group, and Research Councils of the respective National Laboratories.  The evolution of the Projects, thus, have
 gone through a great deal of churning of vast S&T expertise available in the country and also in the concerned
 departments/agencies of the Government.
24.       The Committee was informed that the major chunk of financial allocation (Approx. 72%) is incurred to meet
 requirements of National laboratories, thirty eight in number and its forty seven outreach centres which undertake scientific
 and industrial R&D to maximize economic, environmental & societal benefits for the people of India.  While doing so CSIR
 continuously seeks to foster the organizational value of Excellence in Science.  Global Comptitivencess in technology based
 on high science, local relevance in tune with socio-cultural and economic ethos of the people; and innovation in all spheres
 of activity ranging from Science & Technology to management to financing.  The emphasis is placed on deriving maximum
 output from minimal input.

44.       The infrastructure for most of the CSIR laboratories was built or acquired over four decades ago, some are even of
 older vintage.  Thus, the infrastructure is not suited for modern day globally competitive R&D especially in terms of Good
 Library Practice (GLP), International Organization for Standardization (ISO), National Accredition Board for Testing and
 Calibration Laboratories (NABL) requirements for accreditation and certification.   These are proposed to be refurbished
 through a new scheme of infrastructure renovation.

 all its laboratories.  To some limited extent this could be established, however, the delays in implementation and the radical
 changes in communication set-up since then have made it imperative that it be upgraded into an efficient internet.  CSIR has
 been advising and assisting other organizations to take up computerization and the use of information technology but it has
 not benefited fully from the revolution, except in isolated pockets.  Thus the organizational benefits of the radical gains in
 productivity brought about by IT have not yet been realized.   The IT Task Force has also enjoined that every organization

 students for science. The Committee recommends that the fellowships be given for basic sciences as fewer students are
 showing interest in them.  It is hoped that individual record of progress of scholarship holders is being maintained. 
(Para 32)
3.         The Committee commends the Department for emerging as a pioneering institute to achieve number one position in
 Indian & Foreign patent filings.  The Committee hopes that the Department would maintain its position.    The Committee
 hopes that CSIR will remain vigilant to safeguard our age old indisputable rights over our traditional knowledge.
(Para 38)
4.         The Committee feels that the Department should take utmost care to closely monitor and assess all ongoing projects;
 and initiate critical assessment of the completed projects for their up-scaling and further advancement, if any. Besides, it
 should organize evaluation of new projects to be taken up.
(Para 43)
5.
                  The Committee feels that to face the challenges coming from research initiatives from developed countries, India
 needs the state-of-art infrastructure and laboratories. The infrastructure should be seen as a strategic national resource and
 funding should be given on a long-term basis so that the modernization becomes a continued process for effectiveness,
 improvement in our scientific growth.  The Committee is of the view that the university laboratories need to be upgraded so
 that a world-class infrastructure is provided for research in under-graduate and post-graduate level so that the interest for
 further research is sustained in young students. This in the long term would facilitate advances in the scientific research.
(Para 48)
6.         The Committee feels that the scientific bodies in India need more interaction with industrial houses and if the
 industrial and scientific communities work in tandem both stand to benefit from the other’s expertise.   In the present age of
 competition there should be proactive approach from the CSIR to reaching to industry for finding sponsor for research
 instead of waiting for industry to approach them.
(Para 56)
7.         The Committee commends the efforts of the company for giving emphasis on indigenous technology. But the
 Committee feels that the Department should make efforts to see that the company continued to pursue the programme of
 Development and Promotion of Technologies appropriate for rural areas.
(Para 61)

 petroleum, help in reduction of pollution in our cities.   The Committee would like the Department to conduct research in
 developing fuels from waste matter and other non-bio-degradable substances which otherwise cause environmental
 degradations.
(Para 64)
9.         In order to address the above problem, the Committee feels that IGIB should undertake All India Coordinated project
 on aeroallergens and human health in different strategic   areas of the country in close collaboration with the Ministry  of 
 Environment and Forests  so that a continuous monitoring of pollen in the country could drastically reduce   their
 concentration  in ambient  air over a long period of time.
(Para 68)
10.       Apart from this, the Committee is of the opinion that since bacteria have the ability to degrade biological wastes, it
 enables pollution control and waste management.   This process can act as energy source.  Hence, the emphasis of the work
 of this Institute should be on anaerobic digestion of vegetable and fruit wastes which is also known as municipal market
 wastes with a mission to achieve:-
3)

4)                  Pollution monitoring mitigation systems and devices.
(Para 69)
11.       The Committee is pleased to know that Institutes programme in Environmental Bio-Technology also includes
 projects for development of know how for monitoring and treatment of effluents and biological wastes by anaerobic
 digestion.   The Committee is given to understand that the know how for monitoring the pollution load i.e. Biological and
 Chemical Oxygen Demands i.e. BOD and COD in wastewater has also been developed at IGIB.  The know how has been
 named as BODSEED and has been validated by Central Pollution Control Board after receiving cross validation by seven
 states in the country.
(Para 70)
12.       Yamuna River is constantly polluted by domestic and industrial wastes.  About 2,700 million Liters of Domestic
 Sewage per day (mld), are discharged, of which more than 60% goes untreated in the river Yamuna.  The problem is
 complicated by the 300 mld of untreated industrial sewage discharge in the river.
(Para71)
13.       The Committee therefore, feels that an Anaerobic digestion method for treatment of sewage waste water is
 undoubtedly a good alternative application of anaerobic   digestion theory. The Committee is of the opinion that with this
 simple,  rapid and cheap technology, it will be possible to treat 3000 (cu.m)   of sewage waste water per day and bring the
 pollution load BoD and CoD within  permissible limits.
(Para 72)
14.       The Committee is also given to understand that presently, research is underway at IGIB to develop pollution
 sensitive BoD Biosensor for rapid estimation of BoD i.e. in 10 minutes as against 5 days by conventional methods for BoD
 estimation.  Hence, the know how developed is a refinement of the existing method in order to monitor the pollution load
 precisely, accurately and rapidly.   The Institute has also undertaken research of total Dissolved Solids (TDS) reduction, a
 major unsolved problem of wastewater management by making a breakthrough in reducing TDS to 10 per cent by using
 biotechnological approach.
(Para 73)
15.       The Committee is strongly convinced that environmental biotechnological research of the institute can prove to be a
 boon particularly for environmental management and control and disposal of municipal market waste, wastewater treatment
 and management, treatment and monitoring of Effluents, for TDS reduction and BoD and CoD estimation for monitoring
 pollution load in waste water.
(Para 74)
16.       The Committee would therefore, like to recommend the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research to explore
 the possibilities of working jointly with the Ministry of Environment & Forests to develop a comprehensive waste

 concentration in ambient air in the country so that the entire issue of waste management and control could be given a new
 dimension.

R E P O R T 
  
            The field of biotechnology world over, as in India, has moved with spectacular speed towards 
developing a better understanding and insight into  life processes and addressing many problems
concerning humankind.  Its impact in the domain of health, ag riculture, environment and industrial 
sectors has given a new dimension to  our development process.  Ther e is a paradigm shift in basic 
research in modern biology; scien tists are moving closer to the f undamental secrets of life and the
application of the knowledge generated.   
2.         The Department of Biotechnology (DBT), under the Ministry of Science and Technology was set 
up in February 1986 to give an imp etus to the development of bi otechnology in the country.  The 
objectives of Department of Bi otechnology include the developmen t of products, processes and
technologies whose large-scale appl ications would result in societal and economic benefits.  The 
biotechnology programmes are implemented thr ough a number of autonomous and statutory
institution/universities by giving  them grants-in-aid. 
3.         Work on transgenic, coupled with pros pecting for new genes from our rich biodiversity, is 
poised to pay rich dividends in terms of new products and technologies for improved production and
enhanced nutritive quality of food, fruit and vegetable crops and reduce post-harvest losses.  Application 
of biotechnology to animal health and productivity  including our marine bi oresources will yield
attractive dividends.  India bei ng a global mega biodiversity hub, c onservation, characterization and 
sustainable utilization this natural wealth through the application of biotechnology assumes priority.   
4.         New generation of vaccines, diagnostic kits and therapeutics, are likely to lead to a major shift in
the healthcare strategy for preventi on, early detection and treatment of  diseases that impose the highest
burden.  Stem cell research has emer ged as a cutting edge area of enormous potenti al for application in 
cancer, autoimmune deficiencies, cardio-vascular and neurological disease and other disorders.  
5.         India is likely to require high quality human resource in the biotechnology sector, as industry and
public sector-driven R&D expands to propel the country into a global power in this sector.  The creation 
of infrastructural facilities, promotion of biotech parks and incubators are some of the programmes taken
up during the year, which have contributed significa ntly to the speedy progress.  The importance o f 
bioinformatics has also increased manifold and the best-performing centres are being upscaled as centres 
of excellence.  
6.         Biotechnolo gy-based programmes for societ y es pecially women, weaker sections and rural

GREEN COWS 
59.       The Committee would like to suggest that a section of resear ch in Biotechnology should 
concentrate on the br eeding of special cows that naturally produce low-fat milk that boost immune 
system which may be termed as ‘g reen cow’ and which are specifi cally engineered to produce less 
methane to help stem global warming.  Green cows  generally deliver low fa t milk that boosts immune
system, improve lactose utilization a nd relive diarrhoea.  Recent adva nces in Biotechnology as what the 
Committee has been given to understa nd have identified gene for milk  fat synthesis th at may one day
allow scientists to selectively breed cows that naturally produce low fat milk.  This will also 
considerably improve the efficiency of the milk production of the cows.  Si nce the green cows are
environmentally cleaner cows they produce less si gnificant amount of methane, which is a majo r
contributor to green house effect, in the atmosphere, second, only to CO2 which generally contributes to
global warming.  Green cow can alter cattle digest ion either by removing microorganisms from thei r 
stomachs that produce methane or by creating microor ganisms that can pr oduce metabolic products
other than methane.  The Committee also feels that  if DBT makes a concentr ation on such type o f
research, the emphasis on food safety  will increase and by increasing the body’s defence mechanism, a 
great section of population could be saved from constant attacks of common incurable diseases.  
  
BIO-TERRORISM 
60.       The Committee recommends  that the Department of Bio-technology should take steps to ensure 
bio-security without  hampering legitimate re search or free flow of information in the field 
biotechnology, first, there must be an increased awareness of risk of Bio-Terrorism among scientists and 
scientific leaders.  In order to  augment awareness about security, the committee woul d like to suggest
for arrangement of training and accr editation programmes that would in crease considerable awareness
and stimulate better communications between scient ific and national security communities.  The 
Committee feels that any Bio-secu rity policies must take a ‘botto m up’ approach by including direct 
involvement of working scientists.  The security provisions should wo rk hand in hand with the progress 
in biological research.  It is th e categorized opinion of the Committee th at the strategies that block the 
publication of certain research mate rials would deter the free flow of  information, impede careers o f
scientists in the field of bio-t echnology and discourage new incumbents  in entering the field of research
in Bio-Technology. 
            The guidelines should, therefore, be developed to allow researches to publish their work without 
providing information that would be useful to Bio-Terrorists.  Universities and other scientific 
institutions as what the Committee feels should deve lop the procedures to monitor scientific activities
and design full proof action plan to prevent any strategic inform ation leakage relating to Bio-
Technology to bio terrorists who w ould in turn adversely utilize th ese information for creating Bio-
Terrorism thereby throwing considerable threat on the very existen ce of human communities by waging
biological warfare. 
            Biological weapons pose a strategic threat mirrored by no other form of attack other than nuclear
weapons.  The Committee feels that as there is no simple solution to bio s ecurity, the Department o f
Bio-Technology must construct a syst em of checks and balances need ed to assure that the growing
power of life sciences is only used to protect life and not to destroy it.

methane to help stem global warming.  Green cows  generally deliver low fa t milk that boosts immune
system, improve lactose utilization a nd relive diarrhoea.  Recent adva nces in Biotechnology as what the 
Committee has been given to understa nd have identified gene for milk  fat synthesis th at may one day
allow scientists to selectively breed cows that naturally produce low fat milk.  This will also 
considerably improve the efficiency of the milk production of the cows.  Si nce the green cows are

involvement of working scientists.  The security provisions should wo rk hand in hand with the progress 
in biological research.  It is th e categorized opinion of the Committee th at the strategies that block the 
publication of certain research mate rials would deter the free flow of  information, impede careers o f
scientists in the field of bio-t echnology and discourage new incumbents  in entering the field of research

providing information that would be useful to Bio-Terrorists.  Universities and other scientific 
institutions as what the Committee feels should deve lop the procedures to monitor scientific activities

Technology to bio terrorists who w ould in turn adversely utilize th ese information for creating Bio-
Terrorism thereby throwing considerable threat on the very existen ce of human communities by waging
biological warfare.

Bio-Technology must construct a syst em of checks and balances need ed to assure that the growing
power of life sciences is only used to protect life and not to destroy it.

R  E  P  O  R  T 
  
            Oceans have always influenced the life and history of mankind. From time immemorial, man has
been using oceans in several ways. According to our mythology, the Gods and Demons churned the
ocean and extracted amrita, the elixir of life. Even in the presen t ages, we get mineral, food and energy 
resources from the oceans. 
            The oceanic part of the world has an area of about 361 million sq km  (that is 71% of the globe),
an average depth of about 3,730 m, and a total volume of about  1,347,000 million cubic km.  The 
deepest part of the oceans is the Mariana Trench (11,516 m) in the Pacific Ocea n.  Compare this with 
the 8,849 m above sea level of the highest peak, the Mt.Everest.  Because of its vastness and interplay of 
processes, oceans control the atmosphere and global climate besides being a vast storehouse of resources
necessary for sustenance of life on  earth. Appreciating the importance of the subject, Government o f
India established Department of  Ocean Development in 1981 with  an aim to create a deepe r
understanding of the oceanic regime of the northern and central Indi an Ocean and also to develop
technology and technological aids  for harnessing of resources a nd understanding of various physical,
chemical and biological processes.  The Ocean policy statement was also enunciated in 1982. 
2.         The Department of Ocean Developmen t is the nodal Department for organising, coordinating 
and promoting development activitie s relating to ocean development in  the country.  The national level 
R&D laboratories, educational institutions and industries assist the Department in carrying out its multi-
disciplinary plans and programmes of national importa nce.  Further, marine research and capacity 
building is one of the key areas of the Department to promot e basic research in marine science for self-
reliance. Hence, the activities of the Department are targeted toward s scientific research and technology
development with orientation towa rds its applications and harnessing ocean resources. The Department
has also the mandate towards inte rnational programmes arising out of  international obligations and
bilateral and multilateral coopera tive ventures to create a technol ogical capacity building and human
resource development for self-reliance.

BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2004-05 
4.         The total budget demand for the year 2004-05 is Rs.230.08 crores which includes plan allocation
of Rs.200.00 crores and non-plan allocation of Rs.30.08 crores. The Plan outlay for 2004-05 is Rs.25.00 
crores more than the outlay for 2003-04. The stat ement regarding alloca tion for 2004-05 and budget 
demands made/approved and actually utilized du ring 2001-02, 2002-03 and 2003 -04 is attached as 
Annexure. The following areas have been identified for focus during the year 2004-05: 
(i)         The approved outlay for the Antarctic Research is Rs.24.00 crores which would be given 
as Grants-in-aid to National Centre for Antarcti c & ocean Research (NCAOR ), Goa for launching the 
24th  Scientific Expedition to Antarctica, carrying out scientific experiments, maintenance of the
permanent research station "Maitr i" at Antarctica and infrastructu re development, operation & manning
of the NCAOR. 
(ii)        In the case of Polymetallic N odules Programme, an outlay of Rs.22 crores has been 
provided. Under this programme, the activities planned include, continuation of survey of nodules in the
Central Indian Ocean Basi n (CIOB) area alongw ith the selected profiles fo r identifying and validating
the trends of higher a bundance of nodules; continua tion of Environmental Impact Assessment o f
simulated sea bed disturbance; re search to upgrade existing mining sy stem in a phased manner with a
view to ultimately mining the nodul es at 6000m depth; development of  unmanned submersible, capable
of operation upto water depth of 6000m; and designing of a remotely  operated vehicle for underwate r
examination and continuation of extractive metallurgy.

POLAR SCIENCE (ANTARCTIC RESEARCH) PROGRAMME 
11.       The objectives of the Antarctic Research Programme are to identify and initiate programmes o f
scientific and economic significance besides establ ishing infrastructure.  The Antarctic Research 
Progamme has been designed to ta ke advantage of the unique locat ion and environment of the icy
continent for understanding the key global processes which are manifested and controlled by this pola r
cap.  Antarctic is a pristine and natural laboratory, which enables th e scientists to study, detect and 
monitor global phenomena, such as th e atmospheric patterns and ocean circulations.  Glaciological and 
geophysical research provide s a clue to the geologica l history and evolution of  the earth.  In addition, 
Antarctica provides a singular platform for conducting studies on so lar terrestrial interaction, adaptation
of organisms, including human beings in the cold  land isolated conditions .  During 2004-05, the XXIV 
Antarctic expedition is proposed to be launched.  This expedition will ca rry out research in the fields o f 
atmospheric, geological, biologica l, environmental, medical and engineering sciences and global
change. 
12.       The success of the Antarctic Programme and sustained capabilities in Antarctic science and 
logistics prompted the Depa rtment to establish the first polar res earch lab of the country at Goa namely
the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR ) in 1998 which is res ponsible for carrying
out all the activities relating to Antarctic expediti ons. The research on polar science and expeditions to
Antarctica was being planned, executed and launch ed annually on behalf of the Department by the
Centre.  The Centre has a specific  R&D mandate in the realm of pol ar science and to coordinate an d
launch Indian Antarctic expeditions.  The Centre ha s a unique laboratory for lo w-temperature research 
on ice cores retrieved from  Antarctica and the Himalayas.  It w ould also have the facility for the 
application of remote sensing tec hniques aimed at understanding the s ea-ice-atmosphere interaction in 
the Polar Regions.  It would also have an Antarctic museum and a database repository on polar sciences.

22.       Although the Committee is happy with the contents and perf ormance of projects under Poly 
Metallic Nodules programme of Department, it is, however, scep tical about the Department’s 
assessment about the preservation of environmental norms for optimal sea ecology at the mining site.   
            The Committee is of the opinion that  before a comprehensive pla nning is undertaken for on-site 
mining of nodule, the Department should prepare an experimental chart about the precise disturbance of
the sea floor at the mining area to  assess its geological and ecologi cal conditions.  The Committee feels 
that while organisms would be de stroyed in the mined area undisturbe d areas would remain because o f
the complex terrain of sea bed which could serve as  biological reservoir for recolonizing the destroyed
section.  
23.       The Committee is of the opinion that dangers arising from the release of underlying heavy metals
when the upper sediment layer is removed, could change or disrupt geochemical systems that has been
stabilized over geological time, possibly creating zones of reduce d oxygen where life would become
impossible. 
            The Committee, therefore, feels that  before mining is initiated, Department must examine the
effect of mining on local animals at the site caused by dragging of plough across the bottom to stimulate
the effects of nodule mining on the se a bed, including the rates at whic h animals of the same species
returned to the disturbed area.  The study should be  done in this respect on mega fauna animals large 
enough to be seen at the ocean botto m.  The Committee is of the opinion  that the effects of mining will 
be greatest on the sea sponges that liv ed directly on the nodules because their habitat will be completely
destroyed.  Other free swim ming species will suffer a considerable  reduction in numbers due to serious 
disruption in food supply.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view that from emerging picture above 
the evaluation of bio-threat exposed by sea bed mi ning is indispensable to  be addressed thoroughly 
before venturing into mining operation and the Commit tee feels that any such evaluation is difficult
without better knowledge of the orga nisms living at the mining site a nd the eco-system in which they 
function.  It is quite appa rent that animals at the site area woul d be killed by the im pact of the mining
vehicle and by resettlement of the se diment cloud that impact of the mining vehicle will raise from the
sea floor.  
            Another potential effect of mining on the ocean floor is the bri nging up of unwanted materials 
during a mining operation i.e. sedi ments, trace metals from nodule waste and cold and nutrient rich
bottom water into the upper ocean. Owing to this probl em, the Committee feels that deep or mid ocean
level will be most desirable area for discharging of  miners waste as it would not be harmful to the
environment.  
24.       The Committee further feels that burial sens itivity of sea bed organism s i.e. the consequences o f
dumping a layer of sediment on t op of them as a direct reperc ussion of mining should be studied
thoroughly by Department as lesson for Environmental Impact Assessm ent of sea-bed mining.  The 
Committee feels such studies c ould be undertaken by the Depart ment through Remotely Operated
Vehicle (ROV). 
            The Committee, therefore recommends  that Department should undert ake critical assessment o f 
different mining technique s and their subsequent effects on Geochemistry  and Ocean Biology and
Department should generate relia ble data for determining the optimal mining techniques i.e. ideal
extractive metallurgy to minimize environmental impacts.  
            The Committee, therefore strongly recommends for constant assessment of environmental 
impact of deep sea-mining by Depa rtment before venturing into ac tual mining operation keeping the 
following into consideration for a meaningful assessment of the impact:- 
(a)                Biodiversity, species ranges and rates of gene flow in the nodule areas;

26.       Worldwide researchers believe that oc eans hold the key to a w hole range of new drugs fo r

continued in an intens ive manner during the 10 th plan period. The Department has fostered the search

bioassay guided screening programmes.

COASTAL OCEAN MONITORING AND PREDICTION SYSTEM (COMAPS) 
30.       Under the Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Pred iction System (COMAPS) Programme, the 
Department of Ocean Development had taken up scientific monitoring of pollution at different locations.
The programme aimed to assess the st atus and likely trends in coasta l marine environment quality and
contribute directly to the developm ent of strategies for maximising the economic benefits derived from
the intelligent and sustainable use of marine e nvironment and resources.  The programme had been
continuing since 1991 for monitoring the level of various marine po llutants and its impacts on marine
fauna and flora of the country. Th e data collected under the progra mme was made available to the
Pollution Control Boards and periodically discussed with them. Any significant increase in pollutants at
a particular location was brought to the notice of the Central Polluti on Control Board for control as well

58.       The Committee is pleased to note that the Depa rtment is mainly using two Ocean Research

more challenging and informative if machineries could dive be yond a depth of 6000 meters.  The 
Committee is therefore of the opinion that for a r eal deep sea study Advanced  Tethered Vehicle (ATV)
is needed by Department which is  an unmanned vehicle equipped with  latest advanced technology and
which can easily undertake researches beyond a dept h of 6 thousand metres.   The most striking 
advantage for using the ATV for underwater research is that it is extremely helpful to make researches at
extreme depth where it is dangerous  for divers to venture.  The Co mmittee is given to understand that 
such vehicles are cost affective and can be used in oc ean abyss with much flexibility.  It is observed that 
the vast majority of the ocean depths are bone chilling cold, completely dark and have ambient pressures
equivalent to the weight of the hundreds of atmosphe res. The exploration of th e deep sea is, therefore,
impossible without a subs tantial investment on la test technology.  The Comm ittee therefore strongly 
recommends that the Department may use Advanced Tethered Vehi cle (ATV) for the purpose of deep
sea research in view of its deep sea advantages and cost effective a pplications.  This vehicle will be 
extremely helpful for researches at  ocean benthos where gr eater variety of biotic  and abiotic elements
are available and a study of which could add consid erably to the store house of human knowledge about
ocean depth.

PRESISTENT ORGANIC POLLUTANTS 
64.       The Committee feels that Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) are the most common sea 
pollutants which are consta ntly affecting the Ocea n environment and optimal  marine ecology.  The 
POPs usually gets generated in th e deep sea environment from the d ead biotic organisms. When the
particles of this organisms get sink in the sea bed, a degradation of organic matr ix occurs and
consequently POPs get released in the surr ounding water.  Under anoxi c conditions, sediments 
containing organic carbon releases contaminants into the surrounding water.  POPs not only affect 
microbial food chain but also coas tal environments which are the most productive areas of the sea.
POPs  are also ubiquitous.  Accord ingly, it is an extreme threat towards maintenance of optimal sea 
ecology and it has high exposure to  humans also.  Keepi ng the gravity of the situation into active 
consideration, the Committee feels that Sagar Purvi and Sagar Pasc himi two ocean research vessels,
which are monitoring research on ocean pollution may also direct a major chunks of their study towards
the understanding of POPs behavior and subsequent control of  the same from spreading on the sea
benthos so that the entire biotic community of ocean flora and fauna could be effectively preserved from
environmental pollution.  
            The Committee also feels that two of the main POP group namely dioxin and furans which are
the principal threat to humanity s hould also be studied as a part of  the pollution control programme by
the Department.

4.         Although the Committee is happy with the contents and performanc e of projects under Poly 
Metallic Nodules programme of Department, it is, however, scep tical about the Department’s 
assessment about the preservation of environmental norms for optimal sea ecology at the mining site.   
            The Committee is of the opinion that  before a comprehensive pla nning is undertaken for on-site 
mining of nodule, the Department should prepare an experimental chart about the precise disturbance of
the sea floor at the mining area to  assess its geological and ecologi cal conditions.  The Committee feels 
that while organisms would be de stroyed in the mined area undisturbe d areas would remain because o f
the complex terrain of sea bed which could serve as  biological reservoir for recolonizing the destroyed
section.  
          (Para 22) 
5.         The Committee is of the opinion that dangers arising from the release of underlying heavy metals
when the upper sediment layer is removed, could change or disrupt geochemical systems that has been
stabilized over geological time, possibly creating zones of reduce d oxygen where life would become
impossible. 
            The Committee, therefore, feels that  before mining is initiated, Department must examine the
effect of mining on local animals at the site caused by dragging of plough across the bottom to stimulate
the effects of nodule mining on the se a bed, including the rates at whic h animals of the same species
returned to the disturbed area.  The study should be  done in this respect on mega fauna animals large 
enough to be seen at the ocean botto m.  The Committee is of the opinion  that the effects of mining will 
be greatest on the sea sponges that lived directly on the nodules because thei r habitat will be completely
Page 20 of 29128threport of Science and Technology
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/128threport.htm

destroyed.  Other free swim ming species will suffer a considerable  reduction in numbers due to serious 
disruption in food supply.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view that from emerging picture above 
the evaluation of bio-threat exposed by sea bed mi ning is indispensable to  be addressed thoroughly 
before venturing into mining operation and the Commit tee feels that any such evaluation is difficult
without better knowledge of the orga nisms living at the mining site a nd the eco-system in which they 
function.  It is quite appa rent that animals at the site area woul d be killed by the im pact of the mining
vehicle and by resettlement of the se diment cloud that impact of the mining vehicle will raise from the
sea floor.  
            Another potential effect of mining on the ocean floor is the bri nging up of unwanted materials 
during a mining operation i.e. sedi ments, trace metals from nodule waste and cold and nutrient rich
bottom water into the upper ocean. Owing to this probl em, the Committee feels that deep or mid ocean
level will be most desirable area for discharging of  miners waste as it would not be harmful to the
environment.  
          (Para 23) 
6.         The Committee further feels that burial se nsitivity of sea bed organisms i.e. the consequences o f
dumping a layer of sediment on t op of them as a direct reperc ussion of mining should be studied
thoroughly by Department as lesson for Environmental Impact Assessm ent of sea-bed mining.  The 
Committee feels such studies c ould be undertaken by the Depart ment through Remotely Operated
Vehicle (ROV). 
            The Committee, therefore recommends  that Department should undert ake critical assessment o f 
different mining technique s and their subsequent effects on Geochemistry  and Ocean Biology and
Department should generate relia ble data for determining the optimal mining techniques i.e. ideal
extractive metallurgy to minimize environmental impacts.  
            The Committee, therefore strongly recommends for constant assessment of environmental 
impact of deep sea-mining by Depa rtment before venturing into ac tual mining operation keeping the 
following into consideration for a meaningful assessment of the impact:- 
(g)                Biodiversity, species ranges and rates of gene flow in the nodule areas; 
(h)                Burial sensitivity of deep-sea animals and their response to the type of disturbance 
caused when nodules are scraped from the se a floor, as well as recovery of marine
organisms in space and time; 
(i)                  Impact on ocean column by rising unwante d materials from mining operation located 
above a mine site; 
(j)                 Natural variability in deep ocean ecosystems over space and time; 
(k)               Access to sea bed data which may be gene rated by Central Data Repository under the
control of Department for accurate assessment of environment for determining the choice
of correct mining technique; 
(l)                  Month to month, year to year  and place to place changes to  be investigated as a furthe r 
means of understanding the environment in which deep sea mining will operate. 
          (Para 24) 
7.         The Committee also recommends that apart from the mining of Po ly metallic Nodules, the
Department should also thoroughly assess the potentials of mining Hydrothermal Polymetallic Sulphides
and Cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts from the Ocean bed keeping in view the export potentials of such
Page 21 of 29128threport of Science and Technology
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/128threport.htm

metals in the international market.  
          (Para 25) 
8.         The Committee notes with satisfacti on that under the Drugs from  the Sea Programme, the 
Department is in the proc ess of doing a commendable work.  The Co mmittee is happy with the fact that 
various steps have been taken by the Department for identificati on of numerous marine organisms
showing enormous potential for extraction of such drugs as are anti-diabetic, anti-viral, anti-fungal, anti-
cholesterol and spermicidal agents for developing new drugs. 
          (Para 28) 
9.         The Committee, however, feels that desp ite these initiatives by the Department, there is still 
enough scope left for extr action of potentially anti-c ancerous drugs from the de pth of the ocean.  The 
Committee is of the opinion that  pharmaceutical uses of micro-alg ae which are a great source o f 
unexplored chemical  compounds, are extremely beneficial for a possible source of noble drugs.  Micro-
algae are primitive single celled or ganisms that live in a variety of environments and have a high
potential for producing noble chemic al structures.  The Committee is given to understand that bulbous
yellow soft coral that disrupts erra tic cell divisions in cancer cells and ocean molds that live in sea
grasses also contains sufficient vi rus killing proteins.  Apart from th is, the sea sponges are also a real 
source for extraction of anti cancer drugs.  Other cancer drugs like Didemnin-B isolated from Sea squirt,
Bryostatin-1 that could be isolated from Bugula, Dolestatin-10 that could be de rived from Indian Ocean 
Mollusk and Dolabella, a Sea hare, are also sources of potential drugs  for the treatment of cancer and
other incurable diseases.  Apart from this, several pain killer compounds could be extracted from
horseshoe crabs from the depth of  the Ocean.  The Committee feel s that if the department takes 
comprehensive action to study the extraction of these drugs, the entire system of curative medicine could
be revolutionized on its path of treating and  curing life threatening ailments like cancer and AIDS.  The 
Committee would however, like to lay down that during the extraction of these drugs particularly from
the sea coral enough precaution shoul d be taken by the Department so  that ecological and biological
damages done to such coral surroundings should be reduced to the minimum so that scientific researches
in the field may not stand on the way of preserva tion of holistic sea-ecol ogy with a preposterous 
consequences. 
          (Para 29) 
10.       The Committee observes that the efforts of  the Department to monitor pollution in the coastal 
areas need to be continued vigorously. The Depa rtment should identify locations for periodical
monitoring alongwith stipulated para meters for diffusion and dispersi on characteristics.  Besides, the
stations for collection of near-shore samples must be  planned with a view to reflect the pollution load 
that was occurring there and the da ta collected should be processed and forwarded to State Pollution
Control Boards for taking remedial measures. 
          (Para 32) 
11.       The Committee also observes that the land- based pollutants effect the marine and coastal 
environment, including estuaries and inshore coas tal waters, which are th e most productive areas.
Therefore, it recommends that  a well-planned and we ll-managed marine wate r quality monitoring 
system is required to predict change s of trends in the qua lity of a particular marine water body so that
curative or preventive measures can be taken to restore and mainta in ecological balance in the wate r
body. Monitoring is needed to ensure that standards and criteria set by the regulatory agencies are met
for the protection of marine water quality. 
          (Para 33) 
12.       The Committee feels that for strengthening o cean research centers, the Department should focus
its efforts in assistin g Universities to cr eate infrastructure f acilities and buildin g u p a skilled human
Page 22 of 29128threport of Science and Technology
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/128threport.htm

resource base in marine sciences. Moreover, marine  science teaching on the su stainability of ocean
space and its resources should be strengthened at all levels, from primary to adult education; in curricula
at university level; in adult e ducation programmes for ocean users (fishermen, seamen, workers in oil
industry, coastal engineers) and for managers of ocean affairs. 
          (Para 36) 
13.       The Committee would like to define th e term Bio Technology as reference to a range o f
techniques for identifying, developing and using the propertie s of living  things  to make products o r 
services, it selects natural strains of organisms that carry desirabl e traits makes hybr ids by fusing cells
from different parental sources, us es chemicals and radiation to creat e mutant strains or genetically
engineered plants, animals and microorganisms to produce specific phenotypic characteristics. 
            The Committee by keeping in light the crux of the above comprehensive definition of Bio-
Technology, is of the firm opinion th at any oceanographic research remains incomplete unless emphasis
is given for a deep study in Mari ne Bio Technology for better aqua  culture and improved sea food
supply and increased potential for commercial and Industrial productio ns of Marine substances through
Marine Scientific Research ha ving potential market value. Th e Committee also advocates fo r
encouragement of advanced studies in the field of Marine Scientific  Research through indepth emphasis
on Marine Bio-Technology Research. 
          (Para 37) 
14.       The Committee is also happy to note that two ot her ocean coastal research vessels namely Saga r 
Purvi and Sagar Pashimi are main ly being used by the Department  of Ocean Development for the
assessment of sea pollution within the Exclusive Economic Zone of India.  
            The Committee would like to s uggest that since the assessm ent of the sea pollution and 
subsequent action plan for dealing with the density of pollution is extremely important from the point of
view of maintaining an optimal sea ecology, it is necessary that indepth re search through these two
vessels should be undertaken for a complete monitoring of the ocean pollution and initiating subsequent
steps to control them.  The Co mmittee accordingly, would like to  advise the Department that 
biogeochemical pump, which are micr oorganisms at the sea surface and which take Co2 from the
atmosphere and convert it via phot osynthesis into the organic carbon of  their cells should be studied in
minute details.  When these Microor ganisms die subsequently or cons umed and excreted, some portion 
of that carbon sinks to these floors where it is buried.  As the entire world is confronting the threat of the 
global warming, understanding this concept of biogeochemical pump is essential because it could extract
huge amount of excess heat trapping Co2 from our atmosphere.  A key clue lies in the tiny interface 
where sea water meets se a floor and this critical chemical  reaction determines how much carbon
dissolves back into the water and how much remains in the sediments.  This is known as carbon flux.  
          (Para 41) 
15.       The Committee feels that if Department undertakes a detailed study on this phenomena of carbon 
flux, particularly within the Ex clusive Economic Zone of the I ndian Ocean, comprehensive knowledge
and essential data could be made  available in establishing the role of the oceans in governing
atmospheric Co2 content and also the quantum of sink of Co2 and other gr een house gases on the sea
floor.  
            Accordingly, the Committee feels th at the aforesaid entire progr amme could be made a success 
only if the following primary objectives are kept before it by the Department:- 
1.      Applying the knowledge and e xperience gained through oc ean research to develop
technology in specific fields  like studies in carbon flux through biogeochemical pump, sea
bed mining, ocean energy etc; 
2.      To assist the ocean scientists in the develo pment of suitable engineering and instrumentation

system of effective study of ocean pollution; 
3.      To develop technology for emerging concept of coastal zone management; 
4.      To effectively coordinate with various technical  institutes and other R&D institutes in the
country for monitoring the entire concep t of ocean pollution through an effective
technological programme;  
5.      And to utilize energy from the ocean waves for producing electricity through power plants as 
an alternative to the conventional sources. 
The Committee therefore strongly advocates the Department to initiate comprehensive
programme to fulfill these objectives as a part of their ocean pollution studies and control.  
          (Para 42) 
16.       The Committee is of the view that th e collection and analysis of primary and secondary
data/information for the locations identified along the coast for zona tion of coastal waters should be
carried out as zonation of coastal waters will be useful in sust ainable management and effective
planning for future developmental activities without jeopardizing coastal habitats. 
          (Para 46) 
17.       The Committee would like the Department  to actively participate in  international events an d
expositions so that our scientists get exposure to the developments and innovations taking place in other
countries.  It will also help in exchanging knowledge about the scientific developments of other nations. 
          (Para 48) 
18.       The Committee commends the activities be ing pursued by the Indian National Centre for Ocean
Information Services (INCOIS) in the field of Ocean information and observations.  However, being the 
nodal agency for providing coastal and ocean data  and value added products to the users, the
Department should monitor the performance a nd work-mechanism of the INCOIS to process an d 
disseminate ocean data and data pr oducts to user communities like fi sheries, weather, climate, ports,
shipping etc. on a regular basis so that ocean weather forecasting is precise. 
          (Para 54) 
19.       The Committee is pleased to note that the Department is mainly using two Ocean Research 
Vessels, namely Sagar Sampada a nd Sagar Kanya for deep sea rese arch.  These vessels are using 
remotely operated vehicle (ROV) and Autonomous Underwater vehicl e (AUV) to study about deep sea
life forms at considerable depth.  However, the Committee feels that scope of deep sea research could be
more challenging and informative if machineries could dive be yond a depth of 6000 meters.  The 
Committee is therefore of the opinion that for a r eal deep sea study Advanced  Tethered Vehicle (ATV)
is needed by Department which is  an unmanned vehicle equipped with  latest advanced technology and
which can easily undertake researches beyond a dept h of 6 thousand metres.   The most striking 
advantage for using the ATV for underwater research is that it is extremely helpful to make researches at
extreme depth where it is dangerous  for divers to venture.  The Co mmittee is given to understand that 
such vehicles are cost affective and can be used in oc ean abyss with much flexibility.  It is observed that 
the vast majority of the ocean depths are bone chilling cold, completely dark and have ambient pressures
equivalent to the weight of the hundreds of atmosphe res. The exploration of th e deep sea is, therefore,
impossible without a subs tantial investment on la test technology.  The Comm ittee therefore strongly 
recommends that the Department may use Advanced Tethered Vehi cle (ATV) for the purpose of deep
sea research in view of its deep sea advantages and cost effective a pplications.  This vehicle will be 
extremely helpful for researches at  ocean benthos where gr eater variety of biotic  and abiotic elements
are available and a study of which could add consid erably to the store house of human knowledge about
ocean depth.

          (Para 58) 
20.       The Committee has been recommending for a Research Vessel for the Department and therefore 
notes with satisfaction th at the sustained efforts of  the Department helped th e project approved.  The 
Committee recommends that this project to procure new research vesse l will be implemented as soon as
possible to enable the Department to do its important work for ocean development. 
          (Para 61) 
21.       The Committee feels that Gas Hydrates ha ve the potential of provid ing energy security to the 
country. Therefore, the Department  should encourage excellence in national laboratories to focus on
niche areas of hydrate research with special emphasis on resource ex tent evaluation and environmental
impacts and development of technology for detection and qualification of gas hydrates in sediments.  
                                                                                                                                  (Para 63) 
  
22.       The Committee feels that Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs)  are the most common sea 
pollutants which are consta ntly affecting the Ocea n environment and optimal  marine ecology.  The 
POPs usually gets generated in th e deep sea environment from the d ead biotic organisms. When the
particles of this organisms get sink in the sea bed, a degradation of organic matr ix occurs and
consequently POPs get released in the surr ounding water.  Under anoxi c conditions, sediments 
containing organic carbon releases contaminants into the surrounding water.  POPs not only affect 
microbial food chain but also coas tal environments which are the most productive areas of the sea.
POPs  are also ubiquitous.  Accord ingly, it is an extreme threat towards maintenance of optimal sea 
ecology and it has high exposure to  humans also.  Keepi ng the gravity of the situation into active 
consideration, the Committee feels that Sagar Purvi and Sagar Pasc himi two ocean research vessels,
which are monitoring research on ocean pollution may also direct a major chunks of their study towards
the understanding of POPs behavior and subsequent control of  the same from spreading on the sea
benthos so that the entire biotic community of ocean flora and fauna could be effectively preserved from
environmental pollution.  
             
The Committee also feels that two of the main POP group namely dioxin and furans which are 
the principal threat to humanity should also be studied as a part of the pollution control programme by 
the Department.

INTRODUCTION 
  
      I, the Chairman of the Department-rel ated Parliamentary Standi ng Committee on Science &
Technology, Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on
its behalf, present this One Hundred Twenty-Ninth Report of the Committee.  This Report deals with the 
detailed Demands for Grants (2004-2005) of the Department of Space (Demand No.89). 
  
2.  In the meeting of the Committee held on the 9th  August, 2004 the Secretary and other Officers of the 
Department of Space gave an overv iew of the various activities of  the Department and the Members
sought clarifications on va rious aspects of the perfor mance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise
the Demands for Grants. 
  
3.  The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers  of the Department for re plying to the clarificati o

REPORT 
  
 India has an impressive array of achievements in the scientif ic and technological fields afte r 
independence. Nowhere is this more apparent than in the arena of Space. India has effectively developed
space technology, applied it successfully for its rapid developments and is presently offering a variety of
space services globally. The Space Technology has allowe d the nation to move into the world of high
technology, a place previously occupied only by more developed nations.  
2.         The Indian space efforts started in th e sixties with the establis hment of Thumba Equatorial
Rocket Launching Station near Th iruvananthapuram for the scientific  investigation of the ionosphere
over the earth’s magnetic equator that passes over Thumba. During the formative decade of 1960’s 
space research was conducted by Indi a mainly with the help of s ounding rockets. The Indian Space
Research Organisation (ISRO) was formed in 1969. Space resear ch activities were provided an
additional fillip with the form ation of the Space Commission and the Department of Space by the
Government in 1972. In th e 70’s satellite programmes like Arya bhatta, Bhaskara, Rohini and APPLE
were conducted. The success of those programmes led to the era of operational satellite programmes like
INSAT and IRS came into being. In dia has come a long way in devel oping a multi fa ceted and multi-
dimensional space programme-which is indigenous, self-reliant and a pplications driven. India is now 
capable of building its own state of the art satellites. Now INSAT and IRS are the major programmes o f
ISRO.

INDIAN LUNAR MISSION-CHANDRAYAN-1 
10.       India has vast experience in developing and launching operational spacecrafts systems for survey 
and management of natural resour ces, meteorological services a nd satellite comm unication.  The 
technologies developed and availabl e now at ISRO can be fully expl oited for embarking on planetary
missions with well thought out scientific objec tives.  The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is 
capable of undertaking missions to moon and other terrestrial planets. 
11.       Chandrayaan-1, India’s first scientific mission to Moon is slated for launch during 2007.  The 
primary objectives of the mission are to expand the sc ientific knowledge about th e origin and evolution
of moon, upgrade India’s technologi cal capabilities and provide ch allenging opportunities to the young
scientists working in planetary sciences. 
12.       The Committee was informed that the  idea of undertaking a scie ntific mission to Moon was 
mooted by the Indian Academy of Sciences and it wa s further discussed by the Astronautical Society of
India.  Based on recommendations of  the scientific community and as a first major initiative, a National
Lunar Mission Task Force was consti tuted by ISRO with leading scient ists and technologists from all
over the country for considering a nd making an assessment of the possi ble configuration and feasibility
of taking up an Indian Moon Miss ion.  The task team conducted a feasibility study and recommende d
the Indian lunar mission detailing sc ientific objectives, instruments to  be flown, launch and spacecraft
technologies that are available and those to be de veloped, setting up of a Deep Space Network (DSN)
station for communication between lunar craft and earth and budgetary aspects.  
13.       The Study Report of the Task Team was reviewed in April 2003 by a peer group of about 100
eminent scientists from various re levant fields of planetary & space  physics, earth science, physics,
astronomy and cosmology and after detailed discussion, the participants unanimously recommended that
India should undertake the Moon Mission. 
14.       The recommendations of the task team were  as follows: 
•        The Indian Moon Mission assu mes significance in the context of the international 
scientific community consider ing several exciting missions in planetary exploration, in
the new millennium. 
•        ISRO has the necessary e xpertise to develop and launch the Moon Mission with
imaginative features and it would be different from the past missions.  Hence ISRO 
should go ahead with the project approval and implementation. 
•        Apart from technological and scientific gains, it would provide the needed thrust to basic 
science and engineering research in the country.  The pr oject would help return of young 
talents to the arena of fundamental research. 
•        The Academia, in particular, the university sc ientists would find part icipation in such a 
project intellectually rewarding.  In this c ontext, the scientific objectives would need 
further refinement to include  other innovative ideas from a broader scientific communit y

distribution of minerals such as Si, Al, Mg, Ca, Ilmenites (FeTiO3, which may retain ³He) and elemental 
chemical species including radioactiv e nuclides.  This could unravel th e mysteries about the origin and 
evolution of the planetary system in general and moon-earth system in  particular. The instruments that 
will be used for the mapping are: 
•                    Terrain Mapping stereo Camera (TMC) 
•                    Hyper Spectral Imager (HySI) 
•                    Lunar Laser Ranging Instrument (LLRI) 
•                    Collimated Low Energy X-ray spectrometer (LEX) 
•                    Solar X-ray Monitor (SXM) 
•                    High Energy X-ray/γ-ray spectrometer (HEX) 
  
In addition to the above Indian payloads, a provi sion of 10 kg is made fo r international/national
proposals on new ideas and experiments.

GEOSYNCHRONOUS SATELLITE LAUNCH VEHICLE (GSLV) 
22.       The Committee was informed that th e second developmental te st flight of India’s 
Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, GSLV-D2, was successf ully carried out on May 8, 2003
from Satish Dhawan Space Centre SHAR, Sriharikota (SDSC SHAR). W ith this second successful test
flight, GSLV has been commissioned to launch 2000 kg class satellites into Geosynchronous Transfe r
Orbit. GSLV-D2 successfully placed  an experimental sa tellite, the 1820 kg GSAT-2, in an orbit of 180 
km perigee and 36,000 km apogee with an orbital inc lination of 19.2 degree with respect to the equator.
The Committee was further informed  that the GSLV project was ini tiated by ISRO in 1990 with the
objective of acquiring launch capability for Geosynchronous satellites. The first test flight of the vehicle,
GSLV-D1, was conducted on April 18, 2001 when the 1,540 kg experime ntal satellite, GSAT-1, was 
placed in a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO). 
23.       In the second test flight, GSLV-D2, the higher payload capability was achieved by incorporating 
enhanced propellant loading in core  solid motor, high pressure engine  in liquid propellant strap-ons an d 
second stage and optimisati on of structural elements . In its present configur ation, GSLV is a 49 m tall
three-stage vehicle weighing about  414 tonne at lift-off. The first stage comprises a solid propellant 
motor (S139) and four li quid propellant stra p-on motors (L40H). It carries 138 tonne of H ydroxyl

(UH25) and Nitrogen Tetroxide (N2O 4). The second stage of GSLV  also uses UH25 and N2O 4. The

provides the required separation velocity. Th e Redundant Strap Down Inertial Navigation
System/Inertial Guidance System (RESINS/(IGS), housed in the equipment bay guides the vehicle from

based Radars. The complete telemetry and tracking of  GSLV from lift-off to satellite injection is 
supported by four gr ound stations located at SDSC SHAR , Sr iharikota and the down range stations at
Port Blair, Brunei and Biak in Indonesia. All th ese stations are networke d with SDSC SHAR during
launch.  
24.       The Committee is pleased to know  that the Department has achi eved self-reliance in space 
transportation and it has accepted all challenges which has come  before it with great passion and
achieved unprecedented success in it. 
CRYOGENIC UPPER STAGE PROJECT (CUSP) 
25.       The Committee was informed that Cryoge nic Upper Stage Project (C USP) envisages design and 
development of an indi genous  restartable cryoge nic upper stage employing liquid oxygen as oxidize r
and liquid hydrogen as fuel for upper stage of GSLV. The endurance test  for duration of more than 16
minutes on the Cryogenic Engine conducted in Dece mber, 2003, which was a si gnificant achievement.
The test involved the fi ring of the Cryogenic Main Engine wi th 7.1 tonne thrust for 1000 seconds,
simultaneously with two 200 kg thrust Cryogenic Steering Engines,  all mounted on a single block as
envisaged in the actual GSLV  flight stage. The steeri ng engines are used to c ontrol the flight path o f
GSLV during the third stage thrusting. The turbo- pump fed, regeneratively cooled engine for the 
cryogenic stage is required to burn fo r a duration of 720 seconds in actual  flight. Earlier, in November,
the engine had been tested for 200 seconds in this configuration. The long duration test conducted in
December marked the conclusion of  the qualification of the engine, which has been tested for a
cumulative duration of 6,000 seconds so far through three hard ware sets. First Cryo Upper Stage
(CUS1) integration has been comp leted during the year excluding th e engine. Two propellant expulsion
tests were carried out on LOX prope llant tank. Integration of CUS2 st age assembly was also initiated
during the year. 
26.       The Committee commends the De partment for achieving the feat  of developing an indigenous
cryogenic engine and hopes that this engine would help India in its lunar mission. 
  
 POLAR SATELLITE LAUNCH VEHICLE (PSLV) 
27.       The Committee was informed that Polar Satellite Launch Ve hicle, PSLV-C5, wa s successfully 
launched on October 17, 2003, from SD SC, SHAR and it placed the 1360 kg Indian remote sensing
satellite, RESOURCESAT-1 (IRS-P6) into a 821 km high po lar Sun Synchronous Orbit (SSO). This is 
the heaviest remote sensing satellite launched by ISRO so far. 
28.       PSLV was initially designed and deve loped to place 1,000 kg class Indian remote sensing
satellites into polar SSO. Since it s first successful flight in Oct ober 1994, the capability of PSLV has
been enhanced from 850 kg to the present 1,400 kg into 820 km SSO. PSLV has also demonstrated
multiple satellite launch capability. So far, it has launched seven Indian satellites as well as four small
satellites for international customers.

29.       The Committee was further informed that  the improvement in the payload capability of PSLV

30.       In its present configuration, the 44.4 metre tall, 294 tonne PSLV has four stages using solid and 
liquid propulsion systems. The first st age is one of the largest solid pr opellant boosters in the world and
carries 138 tonne of Hydroxyl Term inated Poly Butadiene (HTPB) propellant. The booster develops a
maximum thrust of about 4,762 kN. Each of the si x strap-on solid propellan t motors carries nine

33.       The metallic bulbous payload fairing of PSLV protects the spacecr aft during the atmospheric
regime of the flight. PSLV employs a large numbe r of stage auxiliary systems for stage separation,

34.       The Inertial Navigation System in the equipment bay guides the ve hicle from lift-off to

40.       The Committee was informed that the ED USAT programme is planned to provide a sustainable 
distance education service in Indi a using advanced space and ground- based technology. The system is 
primarily meant for school, college and highe r-level education and will  also support non-formal 
education. In the first phase, a pilot pr oject using INSAT-3A and INSAT-3B Ku- band transponders is 
under implementation in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh. In Maharashtra, the Y.B.
Chavan State Open University, Nashi k, will use it for distance educati on. In Karnataka, it will be used

covered in the second phase . It is anticipated that more users will fund the ground r eceiver network in
this phase and build it up to about 1000 classrooms per beam.  
42.       In the third phase, the EDUSAT network will be made operational. Manufacturers and service 
providers are expected to replicat e the systems with funding by the en d-users with technical and

country will be built in the opera tional phase. EDUSAT will be able  to support a total of 25 to 30
uplinks and about 5000 remote terminals per uplink. To  meet the full educati onal requirement of the
country, it may be necessary to assemble a constellation of satellites in a phased manner.

students who cannot join regular classroom education.

47.       Although the Committee is satisfied w ith the progress achieved by Department in IRS

48.       The Committee, therefore, is of the strong  opinion that in order to increase accuracy of IRS data

(b)               Production and distribution of satellite data 
(c)                Design of different data base by taking the help of the latest technology; 
(d)               Processing of remote sensing data using func tional approach towards difficulties being 
faced by Department for  accurate interpretation of the data retrieved; 
(e)                Carrying out constant late st research on Remote Se nsing Technology facilities an d
equipment including sensors and ground stations; 
(f)                 Updating of technology at par with world standards; 
(g)                Promotion of remote sensing applications in co-ordination with universities and research 
centres; 
(h)                Holding adequate training courses for adva nced handling of da ta generation and 
interpretation; 
(i)                  On the  job training of DOS personnel to considerably enhance their scientific 
capabilities; 
(j)                 Co-operation and Co-ordination with internat ional society relating to space science an d
remote sensing technologies; 
(k)               Maintenance of national archive on remote sensing data with a view to preserve data and
also constantly up-dating it; 
(l)                  Planning research Programme s for processing, analyzing and production of remote
sensing data with a primary view to maintain accuracy and quality both in generation and
reading the data; and lastly 
(m)              Setting up of a National Remote Sensing Co -ordination Committee to give a holistic

TELEMEDICINE 
55.       Telemedicine is an emerging applicat ion of satellite communica tions wherein the remote
hospitals and health cent res located in rural and remote areas can be connected to super speciality
hospitals located in the cities. ISRO telemedicine pilot projec t was started in 2001 as technology
demonstration for providing telemedi cine facility to grassroots le vel population. Telemedicine system
consists of customized medical software integrated with com puter hardware, along with medical
diagnostic instruments, connected to the commerci al VSAT (Very Sm all Aperture Terminal) at each
location. The medical record/history of the patient is sent to the Sp ecialist Doctors, who in-turn study 
and provide diagnosis and treatment during video-conference with the patient’s end.  
56.       During the year, 23 additional hospitals we re brought into the telemedicine network bringing the 
total number of hospitals in the network to 50 hospi tals – 36 Remote/District/Medical/Mobile Hospitals 
connected to 14 Super Speciality Hospitals namely;  
•           Four  Islands of Lakshadweep, (Amini, Agatti, Andrott and Minicoy) are connected to
Amritha Institute of Medical Sciences, Kochi. 
•           Five Remote/field/base hospitals of  Indian army are connected to research and referral 
hospital at New Delhi. 
•           STNM Hospital Gangtok, Sikkim a nd Regional Institute of Medical Sciences, Imphal,
Manipur are connected to Asia Heart Foundation, Kolkata. 
•           Mobile Tele-opthalmology Unit fo r the Eye Care Camps with connectivity to Shankara 
Netralaya, Chennai and Bangalore. 
•           Tata Memorial Cancer Centre is connected to the Remote Cancer Centre at B B Barua 
Cancer Centre, Guwahati. 
57.       The Committee was also informed that a  temporary telemedicine facility was set up at Pampa at
the foothills of Sabarimala shrine for the benefit of pilgrims during December 2003 – January 2004. The 
telemedicine network has provided more than 12,500 tele-consultations to the beneficiaries. 
58.       Although the Committee commends the st eps taken by Department to  popularise telemedicine 
concept, it feels that the Department should be more  proactive in popularization of the concept in rural
areas. 
59.       The Committee feels that concept of teleme dicine could be made useful in remote areas only by 
setting up telemedicine centres at  Tehsil level which should be c onnected to hubs through telemedicine
networks.

REPORT 
  
The Atomic Energy Commission (AEC), created by a Governme nt of India Resolution on
August 10, 1948, is the apex body for formulation of pol icies and direction of the programmes relating
to peaceful uses of atomic energy in electricity generation, medicine, agriculture industry and research.
The Commission implements its polic ies and programmes that are mult idisciplinary in nature through
the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), wh ich was formed on August 3, 1954. This year the
organisation is celebrating its Golden Jubilee year. From the si ngle unit, namely, the Atomic Energy
Establishment, Trombay (AEET) in  1957, today DAE comprises five Re search Centres, five Public
Sector Undertakings, three Industria l Organisations and three service organisations and seven out of its
eight fully funded institutes are engaged in basic research. In addition, the Department ’s Board o f 
Research in Nuclear Sciences (BRNS) and the National Boar d for Higher Mathematics (NBHM)
promote research in nuclear and allied fields, and mathematics. 
  
2.         The programmes being pursued by DAE emanate from the following mandate: 
  
¾      Increasing share of nuclear power through deployment of indigenous and other proven
technologies, along with devel opment of fast breeder react ors and thorium reactors with
associated fuel cycle facilities; 
¾      Building and operation of res earch reactors for production of  radioisotopes and carrying
out radiation technology applications in the field of medicine, agriculture and industry; 
¾      Developing advanced technologies such as  accelerators, lasers, supercomputers, 
advanced materials and instrumentation, and encouraging transfer of technology to
industry; 
¾      Support to basic research in nuclear ener gy and related frontier areas of science; 
Interaction with universiti es and academic instituti ons; Support to research and
development projects having a bearing on DAE ’s programmes, and International 
cooperation in related advanced areas of research; and

3.         The atomic energy programmes comprise  three sectors, namely, ‘Nuclear Power Sector’, 
‘Industries & Minerals Sector (I & M Sector)’ and ‘Res earch & Development Se ctor(R & D Sector)’. 
The Plan and Non-Plan outlays of  the Department are formulated  under power sect or, industries an d
minerals (I&M) sector and Research and Development sector. The financial supports for the activities of
the Department are provided by budge tary support. The public sector undertakings of the Department
provide Internal and Extra Budgetary Resources (I EBR) in addition to budgetary support to the capital
and infrastructural developments.         
  
4.         The Nuclear Power Sector of the De partment deals with design, construction and operation o f
commercial power reactors with a ssociated safety in all its phase s.  This comprises building o f 
Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors  (PHWR) and development of Fa st Breeder Reactors (FBR) and
Thorium Reactors on commercial s cale.  Associated waste manage ment and environment monitoring
and technology development relating to operation and maintenance of the reactors also form part of the
programmes. 
  
5.         Industries & Minerals Sector is involved in industrial application of  technologies developed in 
the R&D facilities and includes- pr ogrammes related to nuclear fuel cycle covering design, construction 
and operation of industrial plants for refining ores, fabrication of  fuel, production of heavy water,
instrumentation and control, etc. needed for sustai ned operation of the power reactors; and applications
of radioisotopes, radi ation, laser and accelerator  technology for developmen t in industry, medicine,
agriculture and food preservation. 
  
6.         Research & Development Sector pr ovides R & D support to the Nuclear Power Programme o f 
the Department.  The R & D effort s of DAE are in multidisciplinar y high technology areas.  Significant 
achievements have been made in building technical capabilities in the design, construction and operation
of Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHW R); exploration, mining ex traction, purification and
conversion of nuclear mate rials; production of fuel element for nuclear reactors; pr oduction of heavy
water; health and safety research; development and application of lasers and accelerators; development
of Fast Breeder Test Re actors and related instrumentation; re processing of spent fuels; waste
management and production and use of  radioisotopes, besides basic re search in frontier areas of S&T,
particularly radio-astronomy, molecular biology, condensed matter physics, computer science, etc.
