7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/135threport.htm

country to focus on Research and Development in bioinformatics and high end human Resource
Development. The Committee is awar e that bioinformatics, which is a new branch, tries to make sense
of the colossal amount of data on ge netics and extract useful data from  it for the benefit of researchers.
The Committee therefore recommends that more such world-class centres of excellence should be set up 
in the country to focus on Research  and Development in bioinformati cs and the establishment of the
planned institute on bioinformatics should be expedited.

Recommendation 
The Committee hopes that the acti vities of International Depos itory Authority (IDA) should be

Action Taken by the Department 
The infrastructure at IDA has been upgraded by creating facility for supply of liquid nitrogen and
preservation in a separate building and a security system has also been installe d. A separate cold room

students from different parts of India undergo training for eight w eeks in microbial taxonomy including

(IMTECH), Chandigarh. They have organized two workshops on “Fungal Taxonomy: Classical and

The Department, augmented a pr ogramme in ‘Microbial Divers ity’ in 1998, by constituting an 
“Expert Committee”. The endeavour was to isolate,  characterize, index, cla ssify and preserve the
microbial germ plasm from  various ecological niches includi ng extremophilic. N ovel bacterial and
fungal species have been explored  from marine area;  Himalayan belt; arid z ones; psychrophilic zones;
hot springs and oil spills, by various investigators executing this programme. These have been deposited
in “Microbial Type Culture Collection” at IMTECH, Chandigarh. 
  
Comments 
            The Committee expresses satisfaction at the fact that the infrastructure at the International
Depository Authority has been upgrad ed and post-graduate students from  various parts of the country 
are undergoing training at the centre. The Committ ee hopes that more and more students would be
encouraged to receive training and pursue research in high technology areas.

Recommendation 
            The Committee notes with satisf action the advances made in the area of genomics and gene 
sequencing. Further it hopes that efforts should be taken on programme on functional genomics o f
various crops. A multi-institutional programme on development of crops resistant to viral disease should 
be considered.                                                    (Para 42)

Different ongoing research  projects under Functi onal Genomics in the area of nutritional and
stress genomics, cell signalling, light  signalling, developmental genetics and fruit ripening in crops e.g.,
potato, tomato, rice, chick pea, lathyrus, Arabidopsis, pea and catharanthus are continuin g. Apart from

sequencing of several genes, large number of EST sequences  in Chickpea (about 3000) and
catharanthus (about 500) has been  done. Under the Plan t Biotechnology area, programmes have been
supported on development of horticu lture and plantation crops resistan t to viral diseases. A special
initiative on Solanaceae Genome Sequencing is to be launched shortl y under which a major emphasis is
on development of Tomatoes resist ant to viral diseases. The other crops being studi ed are banana,
capsicum and floricultural species. 
Comments 
            The Committee feels that a large portion of the ag ricultural produce is lost  due to viral diseases 
in the crops throughout the countr y. Though the Department has initia ted programmes to produce some
crops resistant to viral diseases, the Committee feel s that the area of research  needs to be expanded to
include a variety of other crops as well. Further the result of such resear ch should reach the farmers
across the country, so that they can avoid their crop losses. 
  
Recommendation 
            Our country has been facing a serious drought condition, which has dr astically reduced the 
production of food as well as comm ercial crops. The Committee is of  the view that the Department
should take initiatives to tackle the problem s of drought by introducing dr ought resistant crops through
the application of functional genomics. 
                                                                                                                                             (Para
43)                                   
  
Action Taken by the Department 
After the successful completion of the Ri ce Genome sequencing of chromosome 11, the
Department has been supporting projects in the area of functional genomics of rice. The main objective
is identification and functional anal ysis of genes related to yield a nd biotic stress tolerance. The
Department has also suppor ted multi-institutional projects on dehydration stress to lerance in rice:
cloning of responsive genes, their promoters and development of transg enics.  The ultimate objective is
to develop plant transformation vect ors for making abiotic stress tolera nt rice. R&D projects in the area
of crop biotechnology are being supported on molecula r analysis of dehydrati on response in certain
crops.  A joint project on developm ent and evaluation of salt and dr ought tolerant transgenic rice is
being considered under the Indo-US collaborative programme in the area of agricultural biotechnology. 
As regards drought resistance, under the biopr ospecting programme a study has been supported
for identifying genes resistant to  drought from plants of the dese rt regions. Express Sequence Tags
(EST) database is being developed under this project. 
  
Comments 
The Committee commends the role of the Department in producing drought resistant rice variety.
However, the Committee feels that the Department should promote research towards developing drought
resistant wheat varieties and other crops. In this regard the advances made  by other countries facing
droughts can also be taken note of .  
The Committee is also aware of the fact that to mi nimize the impact of drought, soil needs to
retain the rainwater and store as much of that water as possible for future plant use. These conditions can
be achieved through management of organic matter, which can increase water storage by 16,000 gallons
per acre-foot for each 1% organic matt er. Organic matter also increases th e soil's ability to take in wate r 
during rainfall, assuring that more water will be stored. When all th ese factors are ta ken together the
severity of drought and the need for irrigation are gr eatly reduced. Keeping this in view, the Committee
hopes that the De partment would examine the feasibilit y of the aforesaid procedure to minimize the

impact of drought.

GREEN COWS 
Recommendation 
            The Committee would like to suggest that a section of research in Biotechnology should 
concentrate on the br eeding of special cows that naturally produce low-fat milk that boost immune 
system which may be termed as ‘g reen cow’ and which are specifi cally engineered to produce less 
methane to help stem global warming.  Green cows generally deliver low fat milk that boosts immune
system, improve lactose utilization and relive diarrhoea.  Recent a dvances in Biotechnology as what the
Committee has been given to understa nd have identified gene for milk  fat synthesis th at may one day
allow scientists to selectively breed cows that naturally produce low fat milk. This will also considerably
improve the efficiency of the m ilk production of the cows. Since th e green cows are environmentally
cleaner cows they produce less signi ficant amount of methane, which is a major contributor to green
house effect, in the atmosphere, second, only to CO 2 which generally contribut es to global warming.  
Green cow can alter cattle diges tion either by removing microorgani sms from their stomachs that
produce methane or by creating mi croorganisms that can produce metabolic products other than
methane.  The Committee also feels that if DBT makes a concentration on such type of  research, the
emphasis on food safety will increas e and by increasing the body’s defen ce mechanism, a great section 
of population could be saved from constant attacks of common incurable diseases.     (Para 59) 
  
Action Taken by the Department 
The concept of the designer cows and green co ws is one among the many promises of genetic 
engineering  and  recombinant  DNA technology. Producing animal products that selectively suits 
human beings with the specific de mand is one of the goal. Depart ment of Biotechnology has already
supported a programme  on developm ent / standardization of  transg enic  technology in  mice model 
and  more than  20 lines of transgen ic  mice  have  been developed.  Efforts are on to  develop  similar 
programme  in cattle keeping in view of the need  of the country . Embryo tr ansfer  technology  is now
well established in catt le, buffalo, goat, camel et c. through the  support of the Department and the
technology  can be  used to  multiply designer/ elit e animal  at a  faster ra te. A major cattle breeding
programme using DNA mark ers and embryo technology is on the anvil. Selective use of creating
knockdown livestock for undesirable traits without affecting the ba se genetic make  up of livestoc k
population is one of the most important thrust area for which programmes are being initiated. 
  
This De partment has also initiated a programme on ex ploration of unconventional rumen
Page 13 of 17135th Report of Committee on S & T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/135threport.htm

microflora from wild ungulates. Its recolonisation in the rumen of domestic livestock has already
been done. A 1200 lit. capacity reactor  has been desi gned for solid state ferm entation and associated
processes for large scale bioconversion of lignocellulose residues to animal feed. Programmes have also
been supported for selection an d improvement of lignin degrad ing microorganism and Genetic
manipulation of microbes for enhanced ligninase expression. Efforts  would be made to develop specific
programme on identifying microorganism or to de velop recombinant microor ganism that can produce
useful  metabolic  products other than methane. 
  
Comments 
            The Committee notes the steps take n by the Depart ment in initiating research in the area o f
producing animal products that selectively suit human needs. The Committee is of the opinion that since
India is basically an agri cultural country with lo t of cattle population and hence milk production, the
concept of ‘green cows’ holds a lot of promise, especially for the ru ral population.  Further, since ‘low 
fat milk’ has a lot of market poten tial, it can prove to be a boon for the agricult ural and cattle rearing
community. The Committee therefore recommends that the de partment should initia te research in the
aforesaid areas at the earliest and spread the know ledge thus gained among th e cattle rearing population
of the country. 
  
BIO-TERRORISM 
Recommendation 
            The Committee recommends that th e Department of Bio- technology should take steps to ensure 
bio-security without hampering le gitimate research or  free flow of inform ation in the field o f 
biotechnology. First, there must be an increased awareness of risk of Bio-Terrorism among scientists 
and scientific leaders.  In order to augment aw areness about security, th e Committee would like to
suggest arrangement of training and accreditation programmes th at would increase considerable
awareness and stimulate better  
communications between scientific  and national security communities .  The Committee feels that any
Bio-security policies must take  a ‘bottom up’ approach  by including direct i nvolvement of working
scientists.  The security provisions should work hand in hand with the progress in biological research.  It
is the categorized opinion of the Committee that the strategies th at block the publication of certain
research materials would deter the fr ee flow of information, impede car eers of scientists in the field o f
bio-technology and discourage new incumbents in entering the field of research in Bio-Technology. 
            The guidelines should, therefore, be developed to allow researchers to publish their work without
providing information that would be useful to Bio-Terrorists.  Universities and other scientific 
institutions as what the Committee feels should deve lop the procedures to monitor scientific activities
and design full proof action plan to prevent any strategic inform ation leakage relating to Bio-
Technology to bio terrorists who w ould in turn adversely utilize th ese information for creating Bio-
Terrorism thereby throwing considerable threat on the very existen ce of human communities by waging
biological warfare.  
            Biological weapons pose a strategic threat mirrored by no other form of attack other than nuclear
weapons.  The Committee feels that as there is no simple solution to  bio security, the Department o f
Bio-Technology must construct a syst em of checks and balances need ed to assure that the growing
power of life sciences is only used to protect life and not to destroy it.   
                                                                                                               (Para 60) 
                                                                                            
Action Taken by the Department 
The Recommendations of the Co mmittee that the Department  of Biotechnology should take
steps to ensure bio-securit y without ham pering legitimate research and free fl ow of information in the

field of biotechnology have been taken note of and efforts woul d be made to increase the
awareness of risk of bio- terrorism amongst scientists and scientif ic leaders.  The whole issue of bio-
security would be looked into from the viewpoint of bio-safet y, bio-security and information
dissemination and if necessary St andard Operating Procedures w ould be developed. The Department
would set up a small group, which would look into the details of  the recommendations of the
Parliamentary Standing Committee and suggest ways for implementations. 
  
Comments 
            The Committee is of the opinion th at an expert group consisting of eminent scientists and
security experts would be set up at the earliest by the Department to study th e whole gamut of bio-
security keeping in view the security threat posed to the country on account of biological weapons.

         The Committee appreciates the Departme nt for carrying out research  in many frontier areas o f
science and technology.  It is true that science is one of the areas, which can bring leadership and meet
the kind of objectives that India ha s set for itself.  However, the Co mmittee is of the opinion that the

Action Taken by the Department 
  
The suggestions made by the Committee are well taken. CSIR has been proactive in reaching to
the industry. CSIR is the only orga nization which involves industry fr om early stage of development
with a view to build an organic linkage with the industry. Recognizi ng the diversity of activities and
complexity of marketing R & D outputs, CSIR has adopted and put in place a decentralized approach
for marketing the entire knowledgebase generated at  different locations. The laboratories maintain
database of industry relevant to th eir sphere of activities. The laborat ories also make special efforts to
constantly maintain interactio ns with the industries to di sseminate the knowledgebase through
conventional as well as non-conventional approaches, including the print and electronic media. In each
of the laboratory a dedicated group inter- alia acts as a window for the marketing of the entire
knowledgebase of the laboratory. 
  
Comments 
         To realize the full potential of  the efforts involved in  the research and development in the CSI R

Action taken by  the Department  
  
            Disposal of vitrified high level wast e in geological formations has been adopted as a third and
final step of Indian strategy for management of radioactive high le vel waste (HLW) in our three step
approach. The first two steps of this strategy are 
  
1.                  Immobilisation of high level waste in solid form with the objective of  volume reduction 
and reducing the possibility of migration of radionuclides. 
2.                  Interim storage for a period of about 30 years to cool the waste a nd ensure integrity o f
conditioned waste package  by continuous surveillance. 
  
Many of  developed countries in  the world are also following the above three step strategy fo r
management of high level waste.  
  
Disposal of vitrified high level wa ste in deep bore holes or the se a bed is not planned due to the
following reasons. 
  
1.                    Disposal in deep bore holes (about 3000 me tres) is being considered basically  fo r 
disposal of spent radiation sources in  countri es where geological dis posal facility is not 
being planned due to either small size of their atomic energy programme or absence of it. 
In this concept, deep bore holes are planne d and waste is proposed to be disposed and 
sealed with no provision of retrieval. 
2.         In disposal in deep sea bed, there is  a large possibility of loss of control of the disposed
waste and, hence, it is not being considered now. 
  
We agree with the recommendation of the Co mmittee and share the vi ew that disposal o f
vitrified high level waste in deep bore-hoes or in the sea bed would be very costly.

Recommendation 
  
            For minimizing the high level nuclear waste volume for pe rmanent storage and eventually
determining what happens to the ma terial when it leaks out of th e tank, the Committ ee feels, it is
necessary to decrease the waste volume by evaporating as much water as possible from the crusty
sludge.  This will make the transport of the waste easier and storage less costly.   
  
(Para58)
Action taken by the Department  
  
The practice of decreasing the volume of high le vel waste by evaporation is being followed in
our  spent fuel reprocessi ng plants as well as in high level waste vitrificati on facilities. Evaporation by
concentration in specially designed thermo-syphon evaporators is an integral part of the basic flow sheet
of all these plants. We are, thus, able to reduce the waste volumes substantially. 
  
As regards the storage of HLW in  the liquid form, this is done in high integrity stainless steel
storage tanks with cooling and instrumentation provisions. Our experience of HLW storage in tanks over
last more than three decades  is excellent from safety point of view with not a single instance of leakage
of any of the tanks. 
  
In order to avoid transportation of HLW, care  has been taken during the plant design by co-
locating reprocessing and vitrification plants. Transfer of waste among reprocessing plant, waste storage
tanks and vitrification plant is done through underground shielded piping system to avoid radiation
exposure to operation personnel. 
  
Thus, aspects of volume reduction of  HLW, its safe storage and tran sfer are an in tegral part o f
the design of our facilities and their safe performance has been demonstrated during last more than three
decades of operations.

generally in the range of milligm/litre against our requirement of microgm/litre

mines, in sites to be designate d.   The remaining low-level waste may then be encased in cement an d 
stored on site. 
(Para 63)
Action taken by the Department 
Disposal in 1000 feet salt mines is not being considered in India since massive deep salt deposits

            The Committee notes the reply of the Department. 
  
Recommendation 
            Inorganic ion exchangers can also be used in nuclear medicines.  Ra dioactive elements with
short half lives currently are used to determine blood flow or to locate a tumor.   With the ion exchanger,
it might be possible to be tter target the tumor by sparing surr ounding healthy cells.  Inorganic materials
exchange ions more efficiently than organic materials and they can withstand radiation better. 
(Para 64)
Action taken by the Department  
            Process based on ion exchange are be ing  used in our radioactiv e waste management plants fo r
separation of certain isotopes fr om various waste  streams. Inor ganic ion exchanges like naturally
occurring ion-exchanger known as vermeculite have been used ex tensively in India for cesium 
separation from radioactive waste. However, inorganic ion exch angers are used in once - though made. 
They have better radiation stabili ty than organic ion exchangers . DAE has developed organic ion
exchangers for separation of cesium and strontium from  intermediate level alkaline waste. Compared to
inorganic exchangers, these have ma ny superior qualities like very high selectivity for specific isotope
and re-usability after regeneration. This technology has been used for industrial scale application both at 
Tarapur and Trombay. Based on separated 137Cs isotope, design and installation of facility fo r 
encapsulation of cesium in glass matrix as well as fabr ication of assemblies have  been initiated for use
in blood irradiation.  
Therefore, ion exchange proces s is basically employed for sepa ration of various isotopes from
radioactive waste.  
  
Comments  
            The Committee notes the reply of the Departme nt. The Committee is happy to note that organic 
ion exchanger technology has been used for industria l scale application both at Tarapur and Trombay.
Since ion exchange process is pr imarily aimed for separa ting radio-isotopes from  Nuclear wastes, the 
Committee hopes that in future thes e isotopes will be used for the purpose of productive application in
the field of Nuclear Medicine, particularly in the treatment of Cancer.

difficult to develop industrial scale transmutation processes for nuclear waste management.  In any case,

Committee feels that final disposal  of nuclear waste must  not ever cause hazar dous radiation or othe r
damage to the environment or property.

            DAE has embarked upon a long-range pl an for the development of Accelerator Driven System 
(ADS) which, besides other applications, has the potential of use in tran smutation of long lived
radionuclides.  As a preparatory st ep, process development for separa tion of long-lived radionuclides  
from HLW has been taken up. The separated radionuclides will be subjected to transmutation fo r

            In line with the thinking of the Committee, it is the basic objective of radi oactive waste

geological formation must be safe from the point of view of protec tion of human  and his environment.
To meet this objective, a systems appr oach is followed  so that release to the environment is well within

            The Committee notes the reply of the Department. 
  
Recommendation  
  
            The Committee has been given to understand that  the Universal Extraction, or UNEX, process 
which is being studied in USA by Idaho National Engineering and Environmental Laboratory (INEEL)
engineers which is a subsidiary of US Department of Energy has developed the first demonstrated
technology of its kind capable of removing multiple radio active elements from high level nuclear waste
in one step.  Just a sprinkling of radioactive el ements turns volume of a largely harmless waste into
‘high level radioactive waste’ subject to rigorous and expensive storage standards.   
  
            Such waste is a byproduct of nucle ar energy and weapons developm ent and usually contains a
mixture of intensely radioact ive fission products like Stront ium-90, Cesium-137 and long lived 
radioactive elements like plutonium and Americiam plus hazardous and toxic materials. Separating most
of the radioactive elements  from the other materials can shrink volume of high-leve l waste, reduce the 
total disposal cost and minimise potential harm to the people and the environment surrounding it.  The
Committee is of the opinion that an extractant is required that works in one step and removes radioactive
strontium, cesium and other Actinides at once. 
  
            Using the UNEX process, trimming th e volume of high level waste at least twenty fold, each
gallon of waste shrinks to less than a cup and the twenty fold vol ume reduction leads to a corresponding
reduction in disposal costs.  The ma jority of the waste left over afte r a   UNEX sepa ration is far less
expensive to treat and store than the highly radioactive portion. 
  
            The Committee would like to suggest that this unique UNEX process of squeezing the volume of
enormous nuclear waste to  size less than a cup should be studi ed to depth by DAE and Atomic Energy
Regulatory Board (AERB) so that the benefit of the reduction of disposal cost could be enjoyed by the
Department as an economy measure for treating, managing and storing all types of radioactive waste e.g.
low level, intermediate level and high level nuclear waste etc., and a subsequent  feasibility report could
be submitted before the Committee for perusal and examination, partic ularly keeping in view the cost
effectivity aspect  of the project. 
( Paras 70, 71, 72 & 73)
  
Action taken by the Department 
  
In various countries several solvent extraction process have been developed for the separation o f
long-lived radionuclides, Stront ium-90 and Cesium-137 from acidic radioactive waste solution. These 
processes use different types of solvent employing solvent-extraction equipment of different designs.  
  
Universal Extraction (UNEX) process being studied by Idaho Nati onal Engineering and
Environment Laboratory (INEEL), USA employs a large number of  centrifugal  contactors  in a cascade
manner. In this process,  a universal solvent containing Ch roninated Co balt Di carbollide (ChCoDic) 
with polyethylglycol (PEG) to remove 137-Ce sium and Strontium-90 and C arbamoylmethyl Phosphine 
Oxide (CMPO ) to remove long-lived radionuclides is used. 
  
India has developed extens ive expertise during last  four decades in extr action  of uranium and
plutonium from acidic solutions gene rated during spent fuel reprocessi ng. The solvent used is 30%  tri-
butyl phosphate (TBP) + dodecane  in pulse agitated  columns. Plants  based on this solvent extraction
technology are in o peration at Tromba y, Tara pur and Kal pakkam from 1965 onwards. Presentl y,

 Feasibility study for using a “combined solvent extraction flow sheet”, for extraction of Cs 137, 
Sr90 and long-lived radionuclides from various types of liquid waste st reams forms a pa rt of on-going

extreme depth where it is dangerous  for divers to venture. The Co mmittee is given to understand that
such vehicles are cost affective and can be used in ocean abyss with much flexibility. It is observed that
the vast majority of the ocean depths are bone chilling cold, completely dark and have ambient pressures
equivalent to the weight of the hundreds of atmosphe res. The exploration of th e deep sea is, therefore,
impossible without a substantial i nvestment on latest te chnology. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that the Department may use Advanced Tethered Vehi cle (ATV) for the purpose of deep
sea research in view of its deep sea advantages a nd cost effective applicati ons. This vehicle will be
extremely helpful for researches at  ocean benthos where gr eater variety of biotic  and abiotic elements
are available and a study of which could add consid erably to the store house of human knowledge about
ocean depth.                                                                                                                                      (Para
58) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        The Department is already pursui ng the design and developm ent of Unmanned Tethered
Submersible, upto a water depth of  6000m. This programme has been en trusted to National Institute of
Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai fo r implementation. NIOT is in the process of designing and
developing such deep sea unmanned tethered submer sible with the help of a Russian Institute EDBOE,
RAS, MOSCOW. The system is likely to be ready by May, 2005 for demonstration. 
Comments 
        Keeping in view its deep  sea advantages and cost  effective applications, the Committee hopes that 
sustained efforts would be made to develop Advanced Tethered Su bmersible. The Department should
devise better ways and means to achieve the objective.

        The Gas Hydrate programme is progressing at brisk pace and considerable progress has already

PERSISTENT ORGANIC POLLUTANTS  
Recommendation 
        The Committee feels that Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) are the most common sea pollutants
which are constantly affecting the Ocean environm ent and optimal marine ecology. The POPs usually
gets generated in the deep sea envi ronment from the dead biotic orga nisms. When the particles of this
organisms get sink in the sea bed, a degradation of organic matrix occurs a nd consequently POPs get
released in the surrounding water. Under anoxic conditions, sediments containing organic carbon
releases contaminants into the surrounding water. POPs not only aff ect microbial food chain but also
coastal environments which are the most productive  areas of the sea. PO Ps are also ubiquitous.
Accordingly, it is an extreme th reat towards maintenance of opt imal sea ecology and it has high
exposure to humans also. Keeping the gravity of the situati on into active consideration, the Committee
feels that Sagar Purvi and Sagar Paschimi, two ocean research vessels, which are monitoring research on
ocean pollution may also direct a major chunk of their study towards the understanding of POPs
behaviour and subsequent control of the same from spreading on the sea benthos so that the entire biotic
community of ocean flora and fauna could be effectively preserved from environmental pollution. 
        The Committee also feels that two of th e main POP group namely dioxi n and furans which are the
principal threat to humanity should also be studied as a part of th e pollution control programme by the
Department.

Action Taken by the Ministry 
  
The Ministry of Environment and Forests (MoEF) shares the concerns of the Committee. At the 
same time, it would like to inform the Committee that due to innovative efforts of the Central and State 
Governments especially in enlisting the  active participation of the local communities in forest 
conservation and development, appreciable changes in forest cover have been reported by the Forest

Report, Forest Survey of India 2001) 
  
            The Committee may also be pleased to note that the focus of the forestry management has shifted
from State-controlled production to sustainable management with people’s pa rticipation in the past two 
decades. The Ministry of Environment and Forests vide letter no. 6.21/89-PP dated 1.6.1990 outlined the 
principles of Joint Forest Manage ment (JFM) and conveyed  to State Government s for creating massive
people’s movement through involvement of the vill age communities in the protection, regeneration and
development of degraded forests on “Care and Share” basi s. Further, through it s letters No. 22-8/2000-
JFM (FPD) dated 21.2.2000 and 24.12.2002, this Ministry issued the gui delines for strengthening of the
JFM programme. These letters provided the framework for the Stat e Governments to ensure meaningful
participation of women in JFM programme, extension of JFM in good forests areas, dovetailing o f
village-level forest management microplan under JFM with the Work ing Plan of the forest division, and
formalizing relationships with local village  community by way of signing of Memorandum o f
Understanding (MoU) for JFM.    
            As on date, all 28 State Govern ments have adopted JFM as their key policy relating to
conservation and development of forests.  As per available in formation on 10.9.2003, there were 84632
JFM committees in the country looking after 17.33 million ha. of forest lands (except Meghalaya, which
adopted JFM after 10.9.2003), which is approximately 23% of the total forest area of the country.  
            Tribal and women are the special focus groups under JFM. Almost 60percent of the forest cove r
in the country as per assessment by Forest Survey of India 2001 is availa ble in the tribal districts of the
country, and the tribal families ar e automatically covered in the JFM programme in these areas. As on
10.9.2003, approximately 8.4 million fa milies were involved in JFM programme out of which

Recommendation 
The Committee has observed that given the present state of Wild Life Conservation in India,
there are a lot of work to be done in the field to gi ve the word ‘Conservation’ a real meaning.  Over the
years, the Committee has noted that  the basic requirements for conserva tion of wild life have not been
fulfilled to its best by the Minist ry of Environment & Forests and neither much importance has been
attached for the preserva tion of endangered species of animal and flora which constitute the heart o f
nature in India. 
            In order to give a thrust to the real  understanding of the meaning of  the term ‘Conservation’, the 
term Wild Life will have to be interpreted in a different perspectiv e in the broadest sense possible to
include scientific work, field wo rk, planning and manage ment, control of poach ing and illegal trade,
awareness, education and extensi on of work, eco-development, captive breeding and zoo management 
etc. 
            In order to give a more thrust  on the crux of the above definition, the Committee feel that
following priorities for wild life conservation should be designed by the Ministry during the current plan
period:- 
1.                  Control of poaching and illegal trade in wild life and wild life produc ts made of wild life
parts; 
2.                  Development of protected areas network.; 
3.                  Welfare measures for wild life staff; 
4.                  Eco tourism; 
5.                  Wild life conservation outside protected areas; 
6.                  Prevention and reduction of damage to wild life;  
7.                  Establishment of second home for the Asiatic lion in Gir. 
So long as the Asiatic lion population remains restri cted to a single location, it is at constant risk
from catastrophic natural events li ke forest fire, flood, earthquake et c.  Accordingly, efforts should be
under way to establish a second population of this enda ngered species in a suitable animal habitat.  As
per the Committee’s categorised opi nion, Palpur –Kuno in Madhya Prades h could be identified as the 
most viable alternative for this purpose. 
(Para 25)

Legal Protection against Wildlife Poaching and Trade  
  
            Govt. of India enacted a comprehensive legislat ion “Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972”with the 
objective of effectively controlling poaching and illegal trade in wildlife and its derivatives. This has
been amended in January, 2003 and puni shment an penalty for offences  under the Act have been made
more stringent.  
Offences pertainin g to huntin g of endan gered species and alterin g of boundaries of protected
areas. 
  
            For offences relating to wild an imals (or their parts a nd products) included in schedule- I of part 
II of Schedule –II  and those relating to hunting or altering the boundaries of a sanctuary or national park
the punishment and penalty have been enhanced, th e minimum imprisonment pres cribed is three years
which may extend to seven years, with a minimum fine of Rs. 10,000/-. For a subsequent offence of this

the development of forestry sector has to be further strengthened.  In addition of all th ese measures, the

environment in those towns and in improvem ent of water quality of the river Yamuna.  Wherever

Recommendation 
            The Committee is not satisfied w ith the manner in which the zoological gardens are being
maintained in the country. The facilities availabl e within the zoo for cagi ng animals, preserving thei r
ecological surroundings, the basic cl eanliness, the supply of food patt ern for the animals etc. are not
either significantly congenial or  are not conforming to the ethos  and requirements that an ideal
zoological garden. Zoos neither fulf ill the requirements for emanation of  the idea of conservation of the
wild life in an effective manner amon g the civil population nor do the y carry message of ‘think green’

among the visitors. The Committee feels that the entire  issue should be perused in a different frame o f
perspective to bring out the following in a holistic manner:   
The mission of an ideal zoological  garden should be to conserve , exhibit and interpret a living
collection in order to promote public recreati on, understanding of the relationships between man
and animal and action to sustain the environment we  share. In order to give a perfect thrust to
drive home the crux of the above definition, the zoo should be organised in such a manner that it
should talk about a sustaina ble relationship between the bu ilt environment and natural
environment and the same should be interpreted in a functional manner to the public. The basic
structures of the zoos should be designed in such a manner that th ese could be used as a vehicle

positioned from the very entrance to the deep interi or of the zoo so that it can constantly infuse
environmentally sound themes combined with en ergy efficient performa nce of the building, o f
the animals, water conservation a nd use of natural sun light as light source coupled with careful
selection of basic building materials in the zoo that minimize adverse impact on the environment.
In order to infuse a real thrust to the pict ure, the Committee feels that poly steel insulated
concrete forums could be used which are environmentally sensitive and friendly for construction
of animal confinements.

follows:-

to the community through education and action”.

PROTECTION OF TAJ MAHAL 
Recommendation 
The Taj Mahal at Agra is  one of the most important monuments  of not only in India but also the
whole world.  In recent years owing to  growth of satellite industries, the ambient air quality particularly
within the Taj Trapezium Area (TTZ) has become more and more vulnerabl e to severe pollution
generating a serious threat to the qua lity of white marble stones of this  remarkable structure. This most
celebrated monuments viewed from  a distance, looms on the banks of  a stinking river almost always
enveloped in a haze of dust and smog from be lching smokestacks and exhaust fumes from the
surrounding industries.  The Committeefeels with a painful heart that this soot and fumes will eventually
turn the gleaming white building black. 
It is, therefore, obvious from the above, that in the recent year s the corrosive impact of the
polluted air on Taj Mahal ha s become a matter of grave concern.  Accordingly, the committee feels that
corrosive impact of pollutants and emissions from surroundings industrial conclave and running vehicles
within the vicinity of the monument is required to be addressed on extreme priority basis. 
(Para 82)

of polluting industries;

REPORT
 
The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) is a part of the Ministry of Science and Technology with
 the mandate of indigenous technology promotion, development, utilization and transfer. Establishment of the Council of
 Scientific & Industrial Research in 1942 was a landmark event in the quest for using science and technology for national

2.         The primary endeavour of DSIR is to encourage industry to increase their share in country’s R&D expenditure, support
 a larger cross section of small and medium industrial units to develop state-of-the art globally competitive technologies of
 high commercial potential, catalyze faster commercialization of lab-scale R&D, enhance the share of technology intensive
 exports in overall exports, strengthen industrial consultancy & technology management capabilities and establish user
 friendly information network to facilitate scientific & industrial research in the country.  It also provides a link between
 scientific laboratories and industrial establishments for transfer of technologies through National Research Development
 Corporation (NRDC) and facilitate investment in R&D through Central Electronics Limited (CEL).
 
3.         The above objectives are sought to be achieved through the following during Tenth Plan :
(i)
                    Technology Promotion, Development and Utilization (TPDU) Programmes.
(ii)                  National Research Development Corporation (NRDC)
(iii)                 Central Electronics Limited (CEL)
(iv)                Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)
 
4.         Other activities assigned to the Department are:
(i)
                  Matters relating to International R&D collaboration involving industrial companies and industrial R&D
 centres.
(ii)                International Cooperation/Collaboration agreements with other countries relating to industrial R&D with the
 concurrence of the Ministry of External Affairs.
(iii)               Matters concerning domestic technology, particularly the promotion of ventures involving the
 commercialization of such technologies other than those under the Department of Science & Technology.
(iv)              Matters relating to Technology Trade including exports of Technology and Technical Consultancy Services, in
 close cooperation with the Ministry of Commerce.
(v)                Matters relating to technical, engineering and management consultancy organizations and services.
 
5.         The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research in the Ministry of Science and Technology provides the
 administrative link between the Government of India and the CSIR Society.

COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR)
 
12.       The Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR), a premier autonomous Research & Development
 organization, is a multi-disciplinary, multi-locational set-up, comprising 38 laboratories and 47 regional centres, has
 completed sixty-three years of its existence. Nourished, fostered and supported, since its inception, CSIR is now recognized
 internationally as an institution, which is moving speedily towards achieving global excellence without diluting local
 relevance. In India, it symbolizes a culture that links science with society through technology and industrial infrastructure.
 
13.       The detailed functions assigned to the CSIR are as follows:
(i)
                  Promotion, guidance and coordination of scientific and industrial research in India, including the institution and
 financing of specific researches;
(ii)                Establishment or development and assistance to special institutions or departments of existing institutions for
 scientific study of problems affecting particular industries and trade;
(iii)               Establishment and award of research studentships and fellowships;
(iv)              Utilization of the results of the researches conducted under the auspices of the Council towards the development
 of industries in the country and the payment of a share of royalties arising out of the development of the results of
 researches to those who are considered as having contributed towards the pursuits of such research;

(v)                Establishment, maintenance and management of laboratories, workshops, institutes and organizations to further
 scientific and industrial research and to utilize and exploit for purposes of experiment or otherwise any discovery
 or invention likely to be of use to Indian industries;
(vi)              Collection and dissemination of information in regard not only to research but also to industrial matters generally;
(vii)             Publication of scientific papers and journals; and
(viii)           Any other activity or activities to promote generally the objectives of the Department.
 
14.       As the nation’s strongest holder of intellectual property rights (IPR), CSIR leads the way for protecting traditional
 knowledge strength while adding to the new IPR capital. CSIR was ranked the first amongst major Patent Cooperation Treaty
 (PCT) applicants from developing countries.  CSIR has also continued to promote excellence in science and it  has nurtured
 and supported human technology from 16 to 65 years of age, through numerous schemes on human resource for scientific
 research.  CSIR helped usher India into a scientific milieu, creating and nurturing talent in science, innovation and
 Technology.
 
15.       The creation of major and innovative knowledge networks across and beyond CSIR laboratories, is a key feature of
 CSIR’s performance.  CSIR’s massive network on ‘bio-active molecules’ launched three years ago began the process of
 leveraging the benefit of networking, by bringing together 20 CSIR laboratories and several other institutions.  This
 philosophy has been carried forward with vigour. Most of the programmes for the Tenth Plan have been formulated with
 networking of resources and capabilities as the major component.
 
16.       This year also saw an all-time high in CSIR’s journey so far as science papers, patents and earnings are concerned.  In
 terms of science papers, CSIR published 2188 papers in Science Journals. In terms of patents, it was granted 195 US
 patents(69% of the patents granted to Indians in India). CSIR’s external cash flow was Rs 287.00 crores in terms of its
 earnings.
 
17.       The guiding principle for CSIR during the Tenth Five Year Plan is to provide scientific industrial R&D that maximizes
 the economic, environmental and societal benefits for the people of India.  The Tenth Five Year Plan of CSIR and the Annual
 Plans have been formulated with the background of 8% growth rate envisaged by the Planning Commission and Government
 policy to invest 2% of GDP on Science & Technology.
 
 18.      In the Tenth Plan, CSIR seeks to foster the organizational values of Excellence in science; Global competitiveness in
 technology based on high science; Local relevance in tune with socio-cultural and economic ethos of the people; and
 Innovation ranging in all the spheres of activities from science to technology management to financing.  These principles
 coupled with detailed analysis on strength, weakness, opportunities and threats carried out by CSIR laboratories were taken
 into consideration in deriving the opportunities for CSIR in the market place as well as for socio-economic development.
 
19.       CSIR seeks to usher India into a scientific milieu, creating and nurturing talent in science, innovation and technology.
 It spawned many organizations, many disciplines and  most importantly  has  served  as  a nursery and  training  ground  for
 most of India’s
talented scientists and technologists. CSIR operates six Plan schemes, namely:
(i)
                  National Laboratories;
(ii)                National S&T Human Resource Development;
(iii)               Intellectual Property and Technology Management;
(iv)              R&D Management Support;
(v)                New Millennium India Technology Leadership Initiative (NMITLI); and
(vi)              ICT Infrastructure, Renovation and Refurbishing.
 
20.       The key feature of CSIR’s programmes during the Tenth Plan is the creation of major and innovative knowledge
 networks across and beyond CSIR laboratories. They have been classified as follows:
(i)         Steering Committee identified Network Programmes in Mission mode
(ii)        CSIR Working Group identified Network Programmes
(iii)       CSIR Core Programmes
(iv)       Programmes for Building up Core Competences & Housing for Scientists
(v)        Ongoing Commitments
(vi)       Infrastructure Renovation & Refurbishment (Civil)
(vii)      Common Minimum Programme – CSIR Inputs & Linkages
 
21.       The Committee appreciates that the CSIR is striving towards undertaking a wide gamut of research and developmental
 activities in the area of high technology, which would help in projecting India as a forerunner amongst scientifically advanced

 nations. The Committee, however, feels that emphasis of CSIR should be dissemenation of new technologies from the
 laboratories for the benefit of the common man.
 
NATIONAL LABORATORIES
 
22.       National Laboratory scheme is operated through 38 National Laboratories and 47 field Centres. The research
 programmes/project/activities of the National Laboratories have been categorized into thirteen major socio-economic sectors
 viz.  Aerospace, Biology and Biotechnology, Chemicals, Earth Resources and Natural Hazards Mitigation, Ecology &
 Environment, Electronics and Instrumentation, Energy, Food & Food processing, Health Care, Drugs & Pharmaceuticals,
 Housing & Construction, Information Dissemination and Products, Leather, Materials, Metals, Minerals and Manufacturing.
 
23.       Basic research is the major source of advancement of knowledge in science and provides the foundation for
 development of newer generic technologies for the future. CSIR has to continuously upgrade its core competencies and
 research areas to be planned so as to provide the needed strength for successfully competing in emerging technologies for the
 years to come. The core competencies to be continuously developed are in the areas of aerospace science & technology,
 modern biology and biotechnology, chemistry, geophysics, oceanography, material science, computer aided studies, expert
 system, parallel computation etc. Since the CSIR infrastructure was built or acquired more than thirty years ago, selective
 refurbishment and renovation of existing infrastructure will be carried out during the 2005-2006.
 
24.       The Committee has also been informed that the budgetary allocation  of                  Rs.1054.43 crores for 2005-2006 is
 to meet the ongoing and new commitments of the 38 National Laboratories and its out reach centers which undertake
 scientific & industrial R&D to maximize economic, environmental and societal benefits for the people of India.  In the Tenth
 Plan CSIR seeks to foster the organizational value of excellence in science, global competitiveness in technology based on
 high science local relevance in tune with socio-cultural and economic ethos of the people and innovation ranging in all
 spheres of activity from S&T to management to financing.  During the Tenth Plan CSIR is implementing several programmes
 in network mode and this increase is essentially to provide support to the approved projects during the Tenth Plan. The Non-
plan increase of  Rs. 8.86 crore is to partly meet normal increase under salary and other maintenance expenditure.
 
25.       The Committee commends the efforts of the Department to keep pace with the new technologies and to project the
 country as a technologically developed nation. The Committee feels that keeping in view the fact that the CSIR infrastructure
 was built or acquired more than thirty years ago, building of new infrastructure and renovation of the existing ones are of
 utmost importance and should be taken up in right earnest.
 
RESEARCH SCHEMES, SCHOLARSHIPS AND FELLOWSHIPS
26.       The Committee has been informed that the CSIR has always strived towards promoting and fostering the upgradation
 of the stock of qualified, highly specialized scientists/engineers and technologists in Research and Development in all the
 disciplines of Science and Technology in the country by encouraging and promoting research in the universities and
 institutions of higher learning and support organizations and by supporting organizations to hold symposia/seminars and
 conferences for promotion of scientific temper.
 
27.       The Committee has been further informed that CSIR is highly concerned with the gradual declining interest in science
 education and R&D as a career amongst young talents. To reinstate the glory of science amongst youngsters, various
 programmes and activities are being taken up through a true Team India Parternership, which involves participation from
 eminent scientists and experts from academia, in-house industrialResearch and Development. In order to promote interest,
 excitement and excellence in science education at school and undergraduate levels, each CSIR laboratory has a plan to adopt
 at least one school and one college in its sphere of influence. The laboratory provides its facilities for project work and
 experimentations as well as carrying out student guidance and motivational programmes.
 
28.       In reply to a question regarding the efforts made by the Department to stimulate interest among the new generation
 towards basic sciences, the Committee has been informed that the Department through CSIR is operating a scheme on
 National Science & Technology Human Resource Development through which it provides support to foster, sustain and help
 in upgradation of the stock of the highly specialized scientists, engineers and technologists required for R&D, in diverse
 disciplines of S&T, in the country. The scheme has provided support to the academic community for research schemes, award
 of fellowship and scholarship to young generation towards basics and other sciences. Every year the support is extended to
 new inductees. Around 1200 Junior Research Fellows, 400 Senior Research Fellows, 100 Research Associates and 100 Senior
 Research Associates are inducted, besides support also provided to the existing fellows. A programme to attract the best
 young school children towards science through hand holding was launched in the year 2000 through a CSIR programme on
 Youth Leadership in science where top 100 students of class X level are invited to CSIR laboratories to see the excitement of
 science through live experiments. Besides, in order to promote interest  excellence in science education at school and

 undergraduate level, each CSIR laboratory will adopt at least one school & one college in its sphere of influence. 
29.       The Committee notes that most of the schlorships/fellowships are provided to students at the higher level i.e. PhD/
 Research levels. The Committee recommends that schlorships/fellowships may be provided at the entry level i.e. graduation
 level and may be increased for students in Post-graduate level to stimulate interest among the new generation towards basic
 sciences. The Committee also recommends that the number and amount of fellowships/scholarships should be increased over
 a period of time. The Committee feels that for the development of science there is a need to improve the opportunities for
 well-trained scientists and young talents to pursue innovative research, to educate the next generation toapply science in areas
 of importance for the health, prosperity and security of the nation.
 
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY AND TECHNOLOGY MANAGEMENT
30.       The objective of the scheme is to enhance the volume and value of Intellectual Property (IP) generated by CSIR and to
 share the best innovation and technology management practices organizationally and with the Indian S&T community at
 large. The volume of IP rights secured by CSIR has greatly increased over the time. The major task, however, is to realize
 adequate and appreciable value from the IPR.
 
31.       It is also felt that necessary skills and knowledgebase of those in CSIR engaged in the IPR game need to be
 refurbished, particularly, in some still unresolved issues such as  ‘traditional knowledge’, ‘genomic sequences’, ‘copyright on
 the Net’ etc. It is proposed to advise the policymakers appropriately on the new development and changes proposed in
 international IP rights arena.
 
32.       It has been informed that CSIR’s  position in IP rights arena is quite noteworthy. CSIR has made Intellectual Property 
 as its pursuit, for it continued to be at number one position securing Patents in India and abroad. During 2001-2004, CSIR
 was granted 390 patents in USA, a feat unmatched by any other Indian firm or organization in the country and it has filed
 1223 Foreign and 827 Indian Patents. It is thus by far the largest patent holder in India and ranked at first position along with
 Samsung in PCT filing from developing countries in the year 2002 and ranked third in 2003. It is expected that CSIR would
 be able to file 400 patents in India and 500 patents abroad during 2004-05.
 
33.       For the first time, CSIR instituted the Diamond Jubilee Invention Awards for school going children upto the age of 18.
 A two tier rigorous selection procedure was followed and fourteen inventions were selected for five categories of prizes. To
 protect IP rights, provisional patent applications have been filed for these inventors.
 
34.       In order to refurbish skills within CSIR community a series of awareness workshops/ training courses were organized.
 Significant ones were Capacity building in the area of IP management, Conference cum workshop on the theme Leveraging
 Intellectual Property for Organizational Strategy, advanced IP training program on Negotiating, Contracting and Valorization
 of IP, and International seminar on International Enactments and Practices on Intellectual Property Rights.
 
35.       To expose the participants to the world's current practices on IPR and to enable them to plan their strategies in the new
 IPR regime, the joint effort brought together a team of internationally renowned experts. The seminar provided a unique
 opportunity to the participants to closely interact with Experts from different establishments like Patent County Court, U.K.,
 European Patent Office and Patent Attorneys of leading IPR firms from USA, UK and Japan.For the first time in the country,
 CSIR organized a Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) Users' Meet bringing together users, stake holders and administrators of
 PCT on a single platform to debate as to how users of PCT from developing countries can make the best use of PCT system in
 a cost effective manner.
 
36.       In reply to a question regarding six fold increase under the head ‘Intellectual Property and Technology Management’
 in B.E. 2005-2006 at Rs. 30.00 as compared to R.E. 2004-2005 where the allocation was Rs. 5.00 crores; the Committee has
 been  informed that the increase in allocation has been sought to meet expenses towards capturing, filing, maintenance and
 prosecution of IP generated from the CSIR laboratories/institutes.
 
37.       The Committee commends the CSIR for achieving number one position in securing Patents in India and abroad and
 hopes that the CSIR would strive towards safeguarding the country’s interests, specially keeping in view the efforts made by
 foreign organizations to encroach upon our traditional base.      
 
NEW MILLENIUM INDIAN TECHNOLOGY LEADERSHIP INITIATVE (NMITLI)
 
38.       The NMITLI scheme envisages to catalyze innovation centered scientific and technological developments as a vehicle
 to attain for Indian economy a global leadership position in selected niche areas in a ‘Team India’ partnership. NMITLI

142nd Report of Committee on S&T
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/142ndreport.htm[29-08-2018 16:32:08]
 therefore looks beyond present day technologies and seeks to build, capture and retain for India a leadership position in the
 global arena based on technology by synergising the best competencies of publicly funded R&D institutions, academia and
 private industry. With over 50 private sector companies and over 150 institutes and laboratories networked together, NMITLI
 is the largest public-private partnership in India today.
 
39.       The scheme involves two types of projects viz. (i) nationally evolved and (ii) industry originated. Presently, NMITLI
 projects are spread in, but not limited to the core areas of agriculture & plant bio-technology, bio-technology, drugs &
 pharmaceuticals, bioinformatics, chemicals, materials, information technology & communication, energy and miscellaneous.
 NMITLI is seeking to look beyond these areas for project development.
 
40.       The Committee recommends that a special cell may be set up to coordinate and pool the knowledge gained in the CSIR
 laboratories and the private sector companies and disseminate it through direct interactions with the industry or through the
 print and electronic media. Efforts may also be made to ensure that there is no duplication in the research work carried out in
 the CSIR laboratories and the private sector companies so that country’s scarce resource is not wasted.
 
INFRASTRUCTURE RENOVATION AND REFURBISHMENT
 
41.       The CSIR has translated the S&T goals into viable, low risk and profitable choices. These are multi-location/multi-
institution programme with well-defined tasks. The tasks identified in each programme and their linkages form a matrix of
 inter-related milestones and activities with identified inter-disciplinary teams at different locations/institutions. Managing
 information and computational requirements at various levels in the execution of these milestones/activities is the key to
 success. Therefore, effective and timely access to computing resources across laboratories/disciplines becomes imperative in
 the management of these milestones/activities.
In order to expedite research through network approach the vital components are:
(i)         Strengthening of computation and data resources'
(ii)        ICT support to S&T programmes and R&D areas
(iii)       Inter-laboratory networking
(iv)       Cross boundary information and compute resource sharing
(v)        Information access (intra and inter) laboratory
(vi)       Utilisation of generated knowledge
(vii)      ICT Infrastructure in Labs
(viii)      Monitoring and assessment of CSIR Networked Projects
(ix)       E-enabled uniform system for business development, inventory control, purchases, personnel management and human
 resource development
(x)        Information system to support insight to the R&D issues
 
42.       These requirements necessitate that CSIR set-up an efficient Scientific Knowledge Management System by creating a
 CSIR wide Grid consisting of functional virtual Grids related to areas of concern. These virtual sub-Grids may consist of
 labs/institutes, where specialists and data together form a complete resource in an area of research. These may be managed
 and used systematically to conduct globally competitive R&D.
 
43.       In reply to a question regarding financial allocation for ‘Infrastructure & Renovation and Refurbishment’ for the year
 2005-06, the Department has informed that the allocation during the current year is  Rs.30.00 crore as against a provision of
 Rs.10.00 crore in B.E 2004-05 and R.E. of Rs.1.00 crore for 2004-05.  This allocation is for the Information and
 Communication Technology (ICT) Infrastructure, renovation & Refurbishment of National Laboratories.  The ICT
 Infrastructure & Renovation and Refurbishment is a new scheme of the Tenth Plan for which a detailed proposal has been
 prepared for consideration of the appraising agencies and awaiting their approval.  After seeking “in-principle” approval from
 the Planning Commission, the same would be considered by the Expenditure Finance Committee during next year.  It is
 expected that the proposal would get approved during the financial year 2005-06 and the annual allocation would be fully
 utilized.  The scheme aims to build the basic ICT infrastructure and grid to access and share the resources to support the
 researchers and work on real time and online basis.
 
44.       The Committee feels that India needs the most advanced infrastructure and laboratories for carrying out cutting edge
 research in various fields. The infrastructure should be seen as a strategic national resource and funding should be given on a
 long-term basis so that the modernization becomes a continued process for effectiveness and improvement in our scientific
 growth.  The Committee is also of the view that the laboratories at the graduate/post-graduate level should be upgraded so
 that interest can be generated among the young students for further research.

45.       Technology Promotion, Development and Utilization Programmes (TPDU) essentially endeavours to encourage
 industry to increase their share in country’s R&D expenditure, support a larger cross section of small and medium industrial
 units to develop state-of-the art globally competitive technologies of high commercial potential, catalyze faster
 commercialization of lab-scale R&D, enhance the share of technology intensive exports in overall exports in the next five
 years, strengthen industrial consultancy and technology management capabilities and establish user friendly information
 network to facilitate scientific and industrial research in the country.
 
46.       The broad objectives of TPDU Programmes are:
                        (i)   To promote and support industry efforts towards R&D.
                      (ii)   To encourage R&D system-industry cooperation.
                     (iii)   To support industry for technology development, demonstration and absorption of imported technology.
                    (iv)   To build indigenous capabilities for development and commercialization of contemporary products and processes
 of high impact.
                      (v)   To evaluate the status and performance of technology in selected sectors/areas.
                    (vi)   To facilitate effective transfer and management of technology.
                   (vii)   To promote international technology trade including export of technology projects, services and technology
 intensive products.
                 (viii)   To promote and strengthen consultancy capabilities for domestic use and export requirements.
                    (ix)   To support and use mechanisms, both national and international, towards transfer of technology, both within and
 outside the country.
                      (x)   Generate endogenous capacities for the development and utilization of digital information resources for providing
 inputs to scientific & industrial research in the country.
 
47.       In reply to a question regarding the reasons for the reduced allocation at R.E. stage during the year 2004-2005, the
 Committee has been informed that after the Expenditure Finance Committee approved the TPDU programme in March 2004,
 the operationalization of new scheme at the level envisaged at the time of Budget preparation took time. The financial
 progress in the first two quarters of the year was on the lower side, as the focus during the period was on conceptualization
 and evaluation of different components of the new programme. It involved organization of meetings of experts, to identify
 areas of operation, setting up and organization of meetings, technical advisory committees, advertising of programmes for
 inviting proposals, preparation of brochures, evaluation of the on-going projects, etc.  Thus the expenditure upto the third
 quarter was less.  In the fourth quarter only one-third of the B.E. has been allowed to be spent as per the instructions of the
 Ministry of Finance.  The R.E. was, therefore, reduced to                   Rs. 10.23 crores.
 
48.       The Committee feels that the Department should initiate action to coordinate the research work undertaken by the
 CSIR laboratories and the industrial houses and an atmosphere of co-operation should be generated so that both stand to
 benefit from each  other’s expertise.
 
DEVELOPING NEW GENERATION FUELS
 
49.       The Committee has been informed that CSIR has initiated research activities in the areas of new alternate fuels. 
 Through a network programme on Developing new generation fuel and lubricants, research activities are directed towards
 development of Gas to Liquid Technologies for Dimethyl ether and Fischer Tropsch Fuels; Liquid Fuels and Ethanol
 Production from Biomass; Catalysts for Atmospheric Residue Processing; Performance Evaluation of New Generation
 Automotive Fuels to meet emission norms.
 
50.       Under Hydrogen fuel the research activities are on Thermo-catalytic conversion of Biomass to Hydrogen;
 pyrolysis/decompositon of methane to Hydrogen; application of Hydrogen in Internal Combustion(IC) engine by developing
 Compressed Natural Gas(CNG) Hydrogen Blend and Hydrogen-Ethanol blend.
 
51.       A project on PEM (Proton Exchange Membrane) based fuel cells was initiated under NMITLI with focus on (i) Fuel
 processor for the production of hydrogen; (ii) Cell stack assembly; and (iii) Control & instrumentation systems.  One-
demonstration unit of 5KW based on H
2  reformer with Liquefied Petroleum Gas LPG as fuel has been installed at National
 Chemical Laboratories.  Efforts are on to develop other types of fuel cells.
 
52.       In the area of Biofuels the activities are conversion of non-edible oils like Jatropha curcas, Salvadora, Pongamia,
 Mahdhuca Indica etc. to methyl ester (biodiesel) and its performance evaluation on IC engines; chemical transesterification of
 Oils to Bio Diesel and recovery of By-product; process development of biodiesel (ethyl esters) of jatropha curcas and its
 evaluation on IC engines and field trials on diesel cars; recovery of hydrocarbons from biomass & their conversion to liquid

56.       A project on “Genetic Improvement of Jatropha curcas for Drought Tolerance and Oil Yield” has been initiated under

 for higher survival, adaptability to drought and salinity, high seed and oil yield and optimization of low-cost agro-
technologies for different agroclimatic regions.  This will help address the major issue for making jatropha oil an economically
 feasible alternative to petroleum diesel.
 
57.       The Committee notes that the research regarding biofuels is still at a research stage and commercial production is yet
 to begin. However, the initiative taken by the Department to produce biofuel, specially from ‘Jatropa Curcus ‘ plant is

 from the commercial production of this plant. The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be made towards
 early commercialization of the technology, which will benefit the farmers as well as the consumers.  
 
NATIONAL GEOPHYSICAL RESEARCH INSTITUTE (NGRI), HYDERABAD
 
58.       The Committee is happy to learn that NGRI is developing a special groundwater management strategy for coastal fresh
 water aquifers, endangered by saline incursion and in certain industrial belts for mitigation of groundwater pollution.
 
59.       The Committee is further happy to know that NGRI under a global attempt has taken a lead to prepare a Seismic
 Hazard Map covering the entire Himalayan Belt and Seismically active regions of India, under Global Seismic Hazard
 Assessment Programme (GSHAP).
 
60.       Apart from this, NGRI as a premier institute is handling considerable original researches in engineering geophysics,
 redox-history of the planet and in several important areas of radioactive and geochemical properties of earth.
 
61.       The Committee, however, has noted that in a few prominent areas where research is necessary to understand the
 anatomy of earth’s inner core, the Institute has not so far undertaken any scientific investigation which are as follows:
a)
                  Heat generating capacity of Radiogenic isotopes of potassium which may  power convection in the core of the
 earth and drive the magnetic field in the earth’s crusts;
b)                  The earth’s dynamo action; and
c)                  Geo-neutrino picture of earth’s interior for its better comprehension.
 
62.       The Institute has stated that since geo-neutrino study is not within the purview of NGRI’s research activities, the
 Institute has not attempted any research work in this field.  The Committee, however, sees no reason why such an important
 study has not been kept within the purview of the research activities of the Institute while in other parts of the world the study
 of geo-neutrino imaging of earth crusts is being given primary importance.  The Committee feels that geo-neutrino imaging
 can give vital information about earth’s core that may prove to be extremely useful for Institute’s preparation of Seismic
 Hazard Map on which the Institute has already taken a lead under a global attempt.
 
63.       Moreover, some neglected areas like the understanding of the heat generating capacity of Radiogenic Isotopes and
 greater understanding about earth’s dynamo action may be of considerable help for the Institute to establish a perfect
 intelligibility of the anatomy of earthquake and its accurate prediction which is still eluding the scientists the world over.

NATIONAL RESEARCH DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION (NRDC)
 
65.       The Committee has been informed that the National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) was established in
 December 1953 as a company, under Section 25 of the Companies Act to commercialise the Research and Development
 results of publicly funded R&D institutions as well as to promote the growth of indigenous technology.  The Corporation
 provides comprehensive technology transfer services and acts as a catalyst for transforming innovative research into
 marketable industrial products. NRDC is a unique organization in that and it is the only public enterprise wholly dedicated to
 transfer of technologies from R&D laboratories to industry. During the past five decades of its existence, the Corporation has
 developed strong links and network with various R&D organizations in the country as well as abroad for transfer of
 technologies.  Its operations cover the entire spectrum of industrial technologies ranging from chemicals to metallurgy,
 mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, electronics, biotechnology and so on.  Its promotional and commercial
 objectives are:
                              (i)      Promotion and commercialization of inventions;
                            (ii)      Commercialisation of Laboratory Know-How;
                           (iii)       Financing Technology development;
                          (iv)      Development and Commercialisation of Rural Technology;
                            (v)      Promotion of Export of Technology; and
                          (vi)      Dissemination of Information on Technology Transfer.
 
66.       The Committee has been informed that the budgetary Plan allocation for NRDC is Rs. 1.00 crore for the year 2005-06. 
 It is a premier organization engaged in development, promotion and also acts as a catalyst for transforming innovative
 research into marketable industrial products. Keeping in view the specialized activities of NRDC, the Committee feels that
 the present allocation is too meagre. The Committee, therefore recommends that the Plan allocation should be substantially
 increased from the present Rs. 1.00 crore to at least Rs. 4.00 crores.
PROMOTION OF SCIENTIFIC TEMPER
67.       The Committee has been informed that the CSIR has been organizing, from time to time, training and demonstration
 programmes, workshops, exhibitions and participating in “Kisan Melas’, to disseminate its developed and available
 ‘knowledgebase’.  It would further accelerate these efforts through self-motivated training programmes at identified village &
 taluk levels in association with concerned developmental agencies. In addition, CSIR also published 2188 papers in journals
 for promotion of Scientific temper.
68.       In a country where a sizable population is barely literate, inculcating a scientific temperament and rational outlook is
 not an easy task. However, to improve the quality of life of the people and removing backwardness and superstitious thinking,
 science popularization is of utmost importance. Therefore, the Committee feels that the Department should not only focus on
 the transfer of technologies but also disseminate basic scientific knowledge to the people through various popular media like
 Television, Documentary Films, frequent melas and demonstrations throughout the country.
69.       After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research and assessing the
 various programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs.1557.00
 crores, as sought by the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research for the year 2005-2006 under Demand No.83, may be
 approved.
