Action Taken by the Department
            As per the recommendations of the Committee, NGRI has taken action and conducted feasibility study with
 regard to the points raised by the Hon’ble Members. NGRI’s observations are as follows:
    Earth Dynamo action: It is believed that radiogenic potassium, if present in the earth's core in substantial
 quantities, has the potential to generate heat adequate enough to power earth's geodynamo action. Recent studies
 indicate the possibility of the compatibility of radioactivity in producing earth's early magnetic field, which helps
 in dynamo action. To verify this hypothesis experiments are being conducted at few places in USA and some
 other countries.
    Geo-neutrinos imaging of earth's interior: Geo-neutrinos are produced by beta-decay of radioactive elements
 present inside the earth, in particular, the long-lived isotopes of U238, Th232, Rb87 and K40. It is believed that
 measuring these geo-neutrinos directly will provide information on the magnetic field of the earth and the
 geodynamo. The only attempt to directly detect geo-neutrinos is being attempted using sophisticated low energy
 Kam LAND (Kamioka Liquid Scintillator Anti-Neutrino Detector) facility being built at Honshu in Japan.
 Indirect methods to estimate geo-neutrino flux theoretically are quite ambiguous.
      Both the points raised by the Hon’ble Members are linked, viz., earth’s dynamo action is believed to be
 caused by the magnetic field inside the earth, partly due to heat flow from radiogenic isotopes including
 potassium which produces geo-neutrinos by beta-decay. The concern of the Members is valid and well taken as
 they feel that these studies could be linked to the generation of earthquakes, which are of prime concern to the
 mankind, especially, in view of the recent damaging earthquakes including generation of tsunamis.
    NGRI is already in the forefront of studying the phenomenon of earthquakes and the assessment of hazard
 associated with it so that mankind can be saved from this natural disaster. Several seismological observatories in
 the country are being operated and maintained by NGRI. The preparation of the Seismic Hazard Map covering
 Himalayan and other seismically active regions in India under a Global Seismic Hazard Assessment Programme
 is one such action in this direction. It is now well known that earthquakes occur only up to depths of about 700
 km beneath the earth.  For an earthquake to occur the material has to be brittle.  This is probably the reason that
 earthquakes do not occur at great depths due to increase in temperature and pressure, which makes the material
 more plastic, or fluid in nature.   This molten material inside the earth drives the tectonic plates, which collides,
 and cause damaging earthquakes along collision boundaries and other parts of the earth.  The movement of these
 tectonic plates can be measured using Global Positioning System (GPS), which can provide information about the
 estimates of the rate of movements.  NGRI has already a major program on GPS studies with permanent and
 mobile observation stations.  In the last 5 years, a permanent GPS station has also been installed at the Indian
 Maitri Station in Antarctica. Several  other studies related to seismic structure of the earth are also being carried
 out at NGRI. All these studies directly address the earthquake phenomenon and also lead to the understanding of
 the geodynamics of the earth in terms of the convection in the earth’s interior.
    The concern of the Honorable Members in suggesting these studies seems to address the problem of earthquake
 generation, which is playing havoc with the lives of the people and causing great economic losses. NGRI is
 already addressing this concern by taking up appropriate and detailed studies as per the International
 understanding of the earthquake phenomenon. The studies recommended by the Honorable Members of
 Parliament are very important to understand the dynamics of the planet earth but do not directly address the
 problem of earthquake generation. However the recommendations of the Committee are well taken and in
 response, NGRI has setup a core group of scientists to explore the possibility of initiating the suggested studies in

NATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH INSTITUTE (NBRI), GURGAON
Recommendations
            The Committee understands that although the Brain Research Institute is doing state-of-the-art investigation in the field of various neuro-degenerative disorders and pathological mechanism of
 various ailments relating to human brain, there are still some important areas left where the institute needs to concentrate for giving brain research a holistic
 dimension.                                                                                              (Para 17)                                                                                        
            In the opinion of the Committee, such areas involve detailed investigations into the causes of the fatally life threatening brain cancers like oligodendro glioma, glioblastomas and other forms of
 complicated cancerous brain disorders.           (Para 18)                                                    
             Although the institute is pursuing a research project about the mechanisms of L-BOAA mediated neurotoxicity, the Committee would also like to advocate that research should be initiated by
 the institute regarding secretion of common brain hormones from substantia nigra and artificial development of L-DOPA to deal with basic mechanisms of neuro
 toxicity.                                                                                                        (Para 19)                      The Committee would further like to suggest that researches on endogenous opiates like enkephalin
 and endorphin should also be initiated for understanding the chemistry of pain for designing a comprehensive pain management strategy in case of certain killer disease like cancer etc.             
                                                         (Para 20)                                                                                                     
            The Committee has also noticed that no substantial research has been initiated on PRIONS (Proteinaceous Infectious Particles) by the institute, a Stanley Pruisner concept, which is the main
 cause of BSE (Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy).  The Committee has been given to understand that due to lack of P-2 containment facility available with the institute, no research is being carried
 on PRIONS and PRIONS related disease.   The Committee urges that since such type of disease may take alarming form in future, primary investigation of the causes of such diseases is the need of the
 hour through development of P-2 and even P-3 containment facility with the institute which at present the institute is lacking.                                                                                           (Para 21)
The Committee also understands that problem of Alzheimer, which is a common form of brain disease, particularly at senile age requires more research  as it is gradually on the rise among civil
 population. Latest research reports in the advanced countries show that real culprit in Alzheimer’s ailment is a copper and zinc build-up in the brain. It is believed by the scientists that accumulated
 metals mix abnormally with a protein called beta amyloid in the brain, oxidizes, literally rust and destroy nerve cells.  Amyloid protein plays a helpful role in the brain: absorbing metals like a sponge. 
 But in Alzheimer’s victims, the metals overwhelm the protein.  Copper mixes abnormally with amyloid, releasing hydrogen peroxide and other toxic chemicals and damage the nearby cells.  Some of
 that protein breaks free, becomes “rogue” amyloid, and mixes with zinc to form clumps that leak more hydrogen peroxide - metals as the real culprits. The scientists are of the opinion that excess
 copper and zinc built up in the brain dissolves the protein clumps in the brains, which has already been experimented in animal model.  Since the disease may assume alarming proportion in future due
 to increased stress owing to phenomenal rise in urban conglomerates and modernization, this aspect of the disease requires deep research so that a target drug for controlling the ailment could be
 designed for future medication. The Committee, therefore, recommends that researches in the following fields need to be given greater attention by the Institute:                             (Para
 22)                                                                
Cure for Alzheimer’s;
i)
                    Researches in the field of PRIONS related diseases;
ii)                   Investigation in the field of pain hormone related issues being secreted from Substantia Nigra by brain like enkephalin and endorphin;
iii)                 Cure for  fatal brain cancers like oligodndrogliomas etc. and
iv)                 Investigation into the causes and cure of Multiple Sclerosis (MS).
Action taken by the Department
            National Brain Research Center (NBRC) has already started work in the area of Alzheimer’s disease and currently evaluating and exploring ways of enhancing the efficacy of traditional Indian
 medicines for potential cure of Alzheimer related symptoms.  The center is also taking steps to initiate research in the area of glioma.  Recruitment of a scientist, who is an expert in this area, is under
 process.  Regarding the other areas of research that the Committee has suggested-pain management, prion related diseases, multiple sclerosis and further research into the area of neurotoxicity, NBRC
 is planning to expand and work on these important brain related diseases as and when the current constraints of resources, including manpower resources, faculty positions and other resource
 constraints, such as availability of P3 research facility are overcome.
Points raised by the Committee
            What has been the progress in enhancing the efficacy of traditional Indian Medicines for potential cure of Alzheimer related symptoms?
Clarification by the Department
Several Indian medicinal plants have been extracted and their efficacy for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease is being evaluated using cell culture and animal models of Alzheimer’s disease. 
 These animals contain some of the defective genes that cause Alzheimer’s disease and they develop the behavioural (loss of memory) and pathological symptoms (formation of plaques) in the brain as
 seen in Alzheimer’s disease.  Using these models, it is noted that some of the plant extracts have the capability to reduce the toxic effect of amyloid βpeptide, which is a key factor in the cause of
 Alzheimer’s disease.
Point raised by the Committee
Is there any blue print made by NBRC to expand and work on important brain related diseases? What has been done to overcome the above mentioned constraints?

Clarification by the Department
NBRC has a vision plan for research on brain related diseases, which is a two pronged approach; (i) to understand how brain disorders are caused and (ii) to find rational therapies and cures for
 brain disorders.  Under the first approach, NBRC has initiated research in the areas of Parkinson’s Disease, Alzheimer’s Disease, Huntington Disease, Spinal Cord Injuries, Japanese encephalitis (brain
 fever) and the neurological consequences of HIV.  In the second approach, NBRC has initiated research on stem cells and this is focussed on the use of stem cells for treatment of disorders, such as
 brain and spinal cord injuries. The development of cognitive re-training paradigms for treatment of intractable epilepsy and post head injury disability has also been initiated. NBRC has tried to
 overcome the constraints by the approval of grant for additional laboratories, which are currently under construction. 
Comments
             The Committee notes the work done at NBRC and hopes that the Centre  would vigorously pursue its research on the brain-related diseases and their cure and develop effective treatment for
 them.
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF IMMUNOLOGY (NII), NEW DELHI
Recommendation
The Committee has noted that although this premier research Institute in the field of immunology has not undertaken any work relating to the production of interferons, it has, however, designed
 an appreciative investigation in the field.   The Committee has noticed that interferons have been implicated as signals controlling the way in which the immune system detects and recognises antigenic
 proteins of viruses, including those viruses associated with certain cancers.  Recent studies have shown that interferon-alpha therapy is beneficial in the prevention of liver cancer in patients with viral
 Hepatitis caused by Hepatitis B and C viruses.  Recently, NII has developed and patented a genetically manipulated mouse model of liver cancer to facilitate in-depth studies of preventive as well as
 curative effects of molecules such as interferons and other drugs.   The Committee feels that once these findings from the interferons research proves successful, it could be shared with other premier
 Oncoligical Research Centres in the country.                                                                                                                  (Para 24)
            The Committee has noted that the Institute has not been conducting any research relating to the treatment of some life threatening autoimmune diseases like Wegener’s Granulomatosis,
 myasthenia gravis and pemphigus vulgaris.  Although the Committee knows that these are rare type of auto-immune diseases among human population, the Committee is, however, apprehensive that
 they may become severely life threatening in distant future due to rapid increase in stress related syndrome owing to unabated urbanization and
 modernization.                                                                     (Para 25)                                                                                                                                                  
            Keeping this in view, the Committee feels that such type of auto-immune diseases also require deep investigation for establishing their causes and cure through promising research projects so
 that some concrete answer to these ailments could   be   designed   by medical science before they assume   any    life   threatening proportion. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Institute
 should consider   primary   investigation in the field of the following auto-immune diseases through the production of ‘interferons’: -
           
i)
                    Wegener’s Granulomatosis
ii)                   Myasthenia Gravis
iii)         Pemphigus Vulgaris                                                                           (Para 26)
 
Action taken by the Department
            Interferon-related investigations, addressing both their production and signaling characteristics, have been initiated.  NII scientists have initiated investigations in the way that interferons,
 particularly interferon-gamma, signals to phagocytic cells of the immune system so as to enable them to overcome the resistance of pathogenic bacteria, such as mycobacteria which cause tuberculosis,
 and protozoa such as Leishmania that cause kala azar.  Researchers at NII are also examining the cascade of signals that allow the immune system to determine whether to make interferon-gamma in
 the course of a T cell response.  This decision is crucial for generating a protective immune response against major diseases, such as typhoid fever, tuberculosis and kala azar.  The pathogenesis of
 autoantibody-dependent auto-immune syndromes such as the ones noted by the Committee depends critically on the formation of autoantibodies, and on their effect on cells such as neutrophil
 leucocytes (in Wegener’s granulomatosis).   Investigations to study some of these issues have been initiated at NII.  The genesis of autoantibodies in humans is being investigated by a genetic
 approach, using hybridomas generated from patients suffering from another, somewhat more common, autoimmune disorder, systemic lupus erythematosus.  The target specificities and the genetic
 structures of these autoantibodies are issues being dissected.  As clinical material becomes available, these studies will be extended to other autoimmune disorders mentioned above.  The molecular
 pathways by which neutrophil leucocytes undergo death in response to a number of stimuli are under active investigation in NII.  As insights are gained, these studies will be extended to autoantibody-
mediated death pathways.
Point raised by the Committee
What are the obstacles in obtaining clinical material to study life threatening autoimmune diseases?  What can be done to remove these obstacles?
Clarification by the Department
Obtaining clinical material for cutting-edge immunological investigations such as enumeration of autoantigen-specific T cell populations from disease states is difficult because large and
 multiple serial blood and tissue samples are required.  This is particularly relevant given that large numbers of clinical samples with well worked – out provenance and clinical as well as laboratory

 follow-up are needed to address the multifactorial nature of such complex disorders.  This poses both ethical and practical difficulties.  The difficulties are rendered severe if the disease is relatively
 uncommon such as the autoimmune diseases under discussion here.  They are easier to deal with if the disease is relatively common, such as diabetes mellitus or systemic lupus erythematosus, on

Recommendation

Recommendation
            The Committee appreciates the contribution of the Centre towards DNA fingerprinting, diagnostics in addition to basic research in related areas. The Committee, however, notes that such
 Centres of excellence are very few in number and recommends that more such Centres should be set-up in the country in near future.              (Para 34)

The Committee would like to have the detailed comments of the Department to its recommendation.

The Department has invited applications to establish Centre of Excellence in the emerging areas of biotechnology. The proposed Centres of the Department are : National DNA Training Centre,

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR PLANT GENOME RESEARCH (NCPGR), NEW DELHI
Recommendation
            The Committee believes that agriculture can be made sustainable only through the use of biotechnology.  Since agriculture is the main source of livelihood for a substantial portion of population
 of this country, improving the techniques used in agriculture will lead to the general upliftment of the quality of life of the rural people. This can only be achieved by developing better varieties of
 plants which are better yielding, having higher nutritional value and are resistant to various diseases and pests, through genetic modification. The Department should ensure that the results of the
 achievements in the laboratories are disseminated to the farmers at the earliest.                                         (Para 37)                                                                                                                                 
Action taken by the Department
            The Department has identified Agricultural Biotechnology as one of its priority areas and has been funding various research and other programmes to promote this area in the country.  The main
 objective of the programme is on improving productivity of crops, reducing their yield losses due to various biotic and abiotic stresses, improving their nutritional quality, etc.  The programme makes
 use of various biotechnological interventions like genetic transformation, engineering male sterility for hybrid seed production, molecular marker aided selection and molecular breeding.  In addition,
 programmes are also supported on Plant Genomics and on cloning and characterization of novel and useful genes.  The priority crops identified for the programme are rice, wheat, cotton, mustard,
 chickpea, pigeon pea, maize, potato, tomato, sorghum, pearl millet, groundnut, etc.

 agro-climate zones in accordance with the RCGM guidelines.  These trials are likely to be conducted in collaboration with the National Centre for Plant Genome Research (NCPGR), New Delhi has

 few selected research institutions for open field-testing of the Pod Borer Resistant Bt. Chickpea and Pigeonpea.  Thus, the Department is making efforts to develop suitable crops and test them in the

Recommendation
            The Committee appreciates that the budgetary allocation for the ‘Biotech Facilities, Centres of Excellence and Programme Support’ has been increased, keeping in view the future requirements
 and the strict implementation of the Intellectual Property Rights rules from 2005. The Committee also commends the Department for earmarking sufficient funds for development of infrastructure
 facilities, which is a prerequisite in the field of science and technology. The Committee hopes that the utilization of these funds would be monitored regularly to ensure their proper
 utilization.                          (Para 40)
       Action taken by the Department
            The progress of the on going infrastructure projects is regularly scrutinized by the Task Force and during the current financial year the Department plans to conduct two meeting of the Task
 Force to monitor the progress of the on-going projects and decide on the funding for new project proposals in the identified thrust areas.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
            The Committee is of the opinion that there is an urgent need to streamline guidelines and procedures for approving genetically engineered pharmaceutical products, as this is a complex process
 involving multiple ministries and regulators that lack systematic coordination. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should set-up an autonomous body like “National
 Biotechnology Regulatory Authority” to approve biotechnology products — and dispense with similar tasks being handled by the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee of the Ministry of
 Environment and Forests.  The proposed authority should also incorporate separate divisions in areas like agricultural products and transgenic crops; pharmaceuticals and industrial products; and
 transgenic food, feed and animal aquaculture.                                                   (Para 42)
Action taken by the Department
            For approving genetically engineered products in the country, the department has already proposed an independent National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority (NBRA) during the
 deliberations of the Mashelkar Committee Report preparation, which has been set up for DNA pharma products.  For agriculture products, Dr. Swaminathan Committee has also recommended the
 same structure.  Once these reports are accepted by the appropriate authorities, the department would make efforts to set-up an independent National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority.  As far as
 dispensing with GEAC of  MoEF is concerned, it is not within the purview of the department as this committee has been formed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.  Once the independent
 NBRA is in place after the acceptance of the two reports as stated earlier, the role of approval of all biotech products would rest with the Authority and not the GEAC, as desired in the report of the
 Committee.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply. It believes that an independent National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority (NBRA) will soon be put in place so that regulatory bottlenecks can be removed
 and single window clearance could be made in case of genetically engineered pharmaceutical products
 Recommendation
            The Committee also recommends that besides clarifying regulatory mechanisms, there should be adequate focus on developing human resources — students specializing in biotechnology,
 researchers, teachers of biotechnologycourses and technicians. The Department should also plan setting up new Centers of excellence in food biotechnology, herbal medicine, molecular medicine,
 biomaterials and devices, and bioinformatics.                                                                                                                                         (Para 43)           
Action taken by the Department
            The areas referred to in the para have already been included as thrust areas in the draft National Biotechnology Development Strategy document.  Accordingly, while considering the new project
 proposals, the Department would encourage setting up of new Centers of Excellence in these specific areas.  Efforts would also be made to generate viable project proposals in consulatation with the
 experts available in these fields.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
Recommendation
The Committee notes that most of the funds allocated for Human Resource Development have been utilized for Graduate/Post Graduate/fellowships. The Committee feels that priority has still
 not been accorded to developing Human Resource at the under graduate level. The Committee recommends that proper resource allocation should be made at the under graduate level in consultation
 with the University Grants Commission and various Central/State Boards of Higher Secondary Education.                      (Para 46)
Action taken by the Department
            In the year 2001, DBT had convened a meeting of the agencies involved in biotechnology education, namely, UGC, AICTE and universities, to discuss the issue of appropriate level for
 biotechnology teaching.  The meeting was chaired by Secretary, DBT and attended by Vice Chairman, UGC; Chairman, AICTE and other eminent educationists.  The general consensus in the meeting

 was that biotechnology teaching at under-graduate level should not be encouraged.  It was felt that the basic knowledge of Life Sciences / Biological Sciences (Zoology, Botany, Microbiology,
 Biochemistry etc) is essentially required to study the multidisciplinary area of Biotechnology at post graduate level.  The recommendation of the meeting not to encourage / support Biotechnology
 courses at undergraduate level was circulated to all the agencies like UGC, AICTE etc.  In addition, it was also recommended that AICTE may consider the Biotechnology courses in engineering
 colleges / technical institutions having strength in Chemical Engineering, Biochemical Engineering, Bioprocess Engineering.  During the discussion on the National Biotechnology Development
 Strategy, the dominant view also has been that at the B.Sc. level there should be general exposure in life science subjects and specialization in biotechnology be considered only at the M.Sc. level. 
 Therefore, DBT does not consider it necessary to support teaching programmes at the B.Sc. level.
Comments
            The Committee decides not to pursue in view of the Department’s reply.    
Recommendation
            The Department of Biotechnology should also devise such a programme so that bright scientists working overseas are attracted back to Indian universities. The Committee is of the view that
 today much of the basic research in India is done in national laboratories, away from universities and this means that the teaching Centres and research Centres are disassociated, a situation that needs
 to be addressed seriously. Attracting young Scientists from abroad and involving them in coordinating the research in India would also tackle the problem of Brain Drain.                                        
 (Para 47)
          Action taken by the Department
            Department of Biotechnology is in the process of developing a programme for attracting bright Indian scientists working overseas to Indian universities.  This issue has also been widely
 discussed while preparing National Biotechnology Development Strategy.  The Strategy provides for the following specific measures in paras 2.1 (v) and (viii).  These paras provide as follows.
●          Para 2.1 (v) : Strengthening of teaching and R&D in life sciences and biotechnology in the university system.
●          Strengthening of R&D in life sciences and biotechnology in the university system will be accorded high priority.  This is considered important for improving the quality of education and
 providing exposure to new technologies for students at various levels.  Specific mechanisms to achieve the goal will include:
 
●          Creation of inter-disciplinary centers of excellence with world class infrastructure in key areas
●          Programme support to encourage inter-departmental networking
●          Visiting Professorship and creation of industry sponsored chairs in partnership with the Department of Biotechnology.
            Para 2.1 (viii): Arresting and reversing brain drain
●          The number of post-doctoral fellowships offered by the Department of Biotechnology will be increased to 200 per annum in order to attract talent.
●          Outstanding young investigator grants in biotechnology will be introduced. This will provide a package including salary support, research grant, equipment and opportunities to attend national
 and international conferences.  The salary support under the scheme will be at par with that of entry-level faculty positions.
●          Information on availability of positions in education/research establishments and industries will be provided on a website to facilitate employment of scientists with specific skills at appropriate
 positions.
●          A data base of scientists working in different areas of biotechnology within and outside the country will be created to utilize the expertise appropriately.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.  It hopes that the above measures will be implemented at the earliest.
 STEM CELL RESEARCH
Recommendation
            The Committee feels that extensive research needs to be carried out in the field of stem cell research specially keeping in view the fact that it can treat many diseases for which there seems to be
 either no cure or the alternate therapies are very expensive.  However, the Committee is of the opinion that as the research in this field is at nascent stage, publicity by various research institutions
 should be avoided.  The Committee is also of the view that research work on stem cell should be undertaken in coordination with all the concerned research
 institutions.                                                          (Para 52)

OUTLAY FOR NORTH-EAST & SIKKIM
Recommendation
            The Committee recommends that as there has been greater emphasis on North-East region, the Ministry should make
 a lump sum budgetary support under one head equal to 10% of Plan funds for the North-Eastern Sector including Sikkim
 and not under separate heads as has been made in this financial year.(Para 5.2)
Action Taken by the Ministry
Ministry of Environment & Forests has been earmarking 10 percent of Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) for development of
 North East Region under Major Head 2552.  A provision of Rs. 123.50 crores out of total outlay of Rs. 1234.91 has been
 made under this Head during the current financial year.  Inadvertently, an amount of Rs. 35 crores, for the scheme
 Gregarious flowering of muli bamboos (melocanna baccifera) has been shown separately under Major Head 2552. It is

Recommendation
            The Committee expresses its apprehension about the success of the Integrated Forests Protection Scheme (IFPS)
 after its transfer to the State Governments.  It is of the view that if money is routed through the State Governments, it may
 not reach to the field level and might be dissipated in other scheme of the State Governments.  Since forest and wildlife are
 not really a priority area with most State Governments and accorded very low priority, other schemes of the State
 Governments like Education, Health etc. may get a major chunk of the State allocation, leaving behind a meager amount for
 the IFPS.  The chances of utilizing the allocation for the basic activities of the IFPS, i.e. mobility (roads and vehicles),
 communication (wireless and computers), combat and self defence (arms) and amenities to the frontline staff are very less.
                                                         (Para 39)
Recommendation
            Moreover, IFPS is of significant importance not only for the maintenance of existing forest cover and natural
 regeneration but also achieving the National goal of achieving forest and tree cover to 25% by 200 and 33% by 2012.  But
 the transfer of the scheme to the States may not help in achieving the stipulated 33% target as some States always complain
 about the hindrance of development activities due to thick forest cover in their States.  In all likelihood, such State may
 refrain from utilizing allocation on the IFPS and money can be utilized for some other purpose.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that IFPS should not be transferred to the State and continues to be administered as a Centrally-Sponsored

Action Taken by the Ministry
Forest Policy and Planning in India is a concurrent responsibility of the central government and state governments. Policy
 and Planning are linked to prescriptions contained in basic national legislation, including forestry legislations. In turn,
 policy shapes legislations in as much as legislations provide the structure and grounds for implementation of policies,
 strategies and priorities. Further, forestry is directly linked to overall land use. Hence forest policy and legislations flow
 from, and constitute a part of the national land use and legislative framework for natural resource management. The
 National Forest Policy, 1988 embodies the principles of sustainable forest management and treats forests primarily as
 environmental and social resources.    Recognizing the role of forests in rural livelihoods and in securing environmental
 security for future generations, the Government of India have formulated the National Forestry Action Plan (NFAP) which
 is a comprehensive work plan for the next twenty years to achieve the goal of sustainable development of forests and also to
 increase the forest/tree cover in the country to 33 percent of the land area as mandated in the National Forest Policy, 1988. 
 The National Forest Policy, 1988 contains essential elements to achieve sustainability of all types of forests, which are
 mainly (i) Increase in the extent of forest and tree cover; (ii) Maintenance, conservation and enhancement of bio-diversity;
 (iii) Maintenance and enhancement of ecosystem functions and vitality; (iv) Conservation and maintenance of soil and
 water resources; (v) Maintenance and enhancement of forest resource productivity; (vi) Optimization of forest resource
 utilization; (vii) Maintenance and enhancement of social cultural and spiritual benefits. The Government of India have
 adopted several schemes under National Forestry Programmes  to achieve Sustainable Forest Management and the national
 goal of one third of land area under forest/tree cover, and also simultaneously forging  linkages with livelihood and poverty
 alleviation issues of forest dependent communities.
2.         The sustainable management of forests and trees can make a meaningful contribution towards achieving livelihood
 opportunities to the people living in and around forests.  In particular : (i) the management, harvesting, processing and
 marketing of wood and non wood forest products can provide opportunities for employment and income generation (ii) The
 adoption of agro forestry practices can increase food production and food security in conjunction with provision of  wood
 products for sale or consumption, provide a source of household energy, and improve soil composition (iii) watershed
 management practices can provide multiple goods and services especially enhanced and sustained water production that is
 important to health and sanitation.
3.         MoEF has prepared comprehensive National Forestry Action Plan (NFAP) for 20 years to achieve sustainable
 development of forests and to increase forest and tree cover upto 33% of geographical area with a cost of Rs.133902 Crore.
 The forest and wild life sector is getting around 30%  financial resources of the required need including the budget at the
 national level and funding from external sources. It is a major constraint in achieving sustainability and thus providing
 required level of livelihood opportunities and incentives to the rural people dependent on forests. If adequate investment is
 made, forest and wild life sector is capable of providing livlihood opportunities to the poorest of the poor who live in and
 around forests.           
4.         As regards attracting investment from private sector, the MoEF is working on developing a multi-stakeholder
 partnership (MSP) for afforestation of degraded forest lands. MSP involves local community, State Forest Department  and
 private industry as partners.

In 1999, MOEF commissioned Bharati Vidyapeeth Institute of Environment Education & Research (BVIEER) to conduct a
 nation wide survey to assess the extent of infusion of environmental concepts in the school curriculum and the effectiveness
 of its delivery in the classroom. Simultaneously, a National Consultation on EE was also organized in January 2000. The
 participants at this Consultation, which included officers from MHRD, MOEF, NCERT, State Government Departments of
 Education, SCERTs, etc. and representatives from NGOs besides educationists, were of the view that instead of teaching
 Environment as a separate subject, a separate space/forum should be created within the School System for integrating the
 various environmental concepts infused/introduced in other subjects. The Study revealed that the extent of infusion of
 environmental concepts into the school curriculum varied from State to State- while it was reasonably satisfactory in some
 States, it was very poor in some other states. It was also observed that appropriate training of teachers was necessary to
 ensure effective transaction of the environmental concepts in the class room. The study also recommended strengthening the
 infusion approach. Based on these recommendations, MOEF launched a pilot project on “Environment Education in School
 System” under the World Bank assisted Environmental Management Capacity Building Project with the basic objective of
 strengthening environmental education in the formal school system. The EESS project was implemented in 15 States in
 collaboration with the State Education Departments and the respective SCERTs for greening of the middle school level
 textbooks and their introduction in 100 schools in each state on experimental basis. The introduction of greened books in
 the project schools was preceded by the training of teachers in these schools.
The EESS project also stresses on hands-on activities. A hands-on Environmental learning program Global Learning and
 Observations to Benefit the Environment (GLOBE) was therefore, launched as a component of the EESS project.  India
 joined this program in August 2000 and has so far trained about 1800 GLOBE teachers from about 1700 schools in the
 country. Teachers of the 100 pilot schools were trained in various protocols for conducting the experiments in four broad
 environmental parameters-Hydrology, Soil, Land Cover and Atmospheric temperature / rainfall.  GLOBE provides a unique
 opportunity to its students to carry out various measurements so that they can learn about scientific protocols and perform
 environmental learning activities, which have already been introduced as theory in the greened textbooks developed for
 EESS project.  
The Ministry had also been interacting with the UGC to ensure coverage of environmental components at the college level
 education. A course module has been worked out through UGC for teaching EE as a separate paper at entry level in all
 streams of undergraduate education.
The MOEF has also launched an initiative to integrate environmental concepts and issues in the Management Education
 Syllabi of various professional Management courses in consultation with AICTE in 2002.  The courses content has been
 examined. Workshops have also been conducted to sensitize the faculty of more than 250 management colleges towards
 environmental issues. A Curriculum Development Workshop was also conducted to develop new curriculum and also to
 develop a resource base for teaching material.  An inventory of the courses offered in India and abroad has been prepared
 along with an inventory of resource material.
Besides the above initiatives, the Working Group constituted by the MOEF in April 2004 for the preparation of a
 Comprehensive plan for Environment Education in school; with members drawn from MHRD, NCERT, MOEF, a few State
 Education Departments and representative of organizations (namely CEE, CPREEC and IES) working in the field of
 Environment Education; has recommended that the MOEF shall take following action in the light of the Hon’ble Supreme
 Court’s directive to all the State Government to compulsorily teach environmental concepts in schools as per the model
 syllabus prepared by NCERT:
MOEF will collaborate with NCERT to facilitate the preparation of the textbooks by developing training modules for the
 textbook writers;
MOEF shall help the state governments in training teachers, master trainers/ resource persons by providing financial and
 technical assistance;
MOEF will play an important role in hands-on activities suggested by NCERT in the model syllabus.
Under the research funding program, guidelines are being framed to pay good remunerations to talented persons working in
 institutes, which do not receive core grant, to do research on environmental issues.

CONSERVATION PROGRAMME
Recommendation
            The Committee recommends that National Mangroves Afforestation Programme should be designed so that new
 research projects on the priority areas of mangroves and coral reef conservation for supplementing Management Action
 Plan of strategically identified mangrove areas is accorded importance.                                                   (Para 70.1)
Action Taken by the Ministry
The Government seek to sustain mangrove forests and Coral Reefs in the country by both regulatory and promotional
 measures. The Coastal Regulation Zone notification(1991) under the Environmental Protection Act(1986) recognizes the
 Mangrove and Coral reef areas as ecologically sensitive and categorizes them as CRZ-I(i) which implies that these areas are
 afforded protection of the highest order. Under the promotional measures the Government has identified 35 mangrove areas
 and 4 Coral Reefs areas on a country-wide basis for intensive conservation and management.
The Ministry of Environment and Forests, for the last several years has been funding research in multi-disciplinary aspects
 of Mangroves and Coral Reefs ecosystems protection, conservation and management at various universities, institutions of
 higher learning, national research institutes and non-governmental organizations. There has been an allocation of Rs. 24
 crores during the X Plan for Mangroves and Coral Reefs, of which a sum of Rs.6.50 crores has been provided for Research
 Projects. The Current year’s allocation for Research in Mangroves and Coral Reefs is Rs.5.30 crores. There is an increasing
 emphasis on close interface between Researchers and Managers in the field. The Primary objectives are to develop
 strategies, technologies and methodologies for better management of mangroves areas in the country.

 and Godavari & Krishna Deltas of Andhra Pradesh. To cover these areas with mangrove species, trenching technique has
 been developed and used by the State Forest Departments with financial support from the Ministry.  In this technique,
 canals are formed so that the high saline soils get regular tidal inundation, excess salts are leached out and the area becomes
 suitable for regeneration of mangroves. A workable design namely ‘modified fish bone channel’ has been scientifically
 demonstrated at Muthupet, Tamil Nadu.  In this design, distribution canals are linked to avoid the blind end points.  The
 feeder canals are at 50 m distance and distribution canals are at 20 m distance. Using this technique, the hyper-saline areas
 have been successfully reclaimed.  Similarly, in the arduous terrain along the coasts of Gulf of Kutch in Gujarat, the raising
 of mangrove plantation has been difficult as the tidal amplitude washes away the planted seedlings.  The Gujarat Forest
 Department with financial support from the Ministry has developed and implemented a ‘raised-bed technique’ in which the
 seedlings are planted on raised beds in parallel rows during the low tide hours.

CLEANING OF MAJOR RIVERS BY 2007 AND OTHERS BY 2012
Recommendation
            The Ministry has submitted that it is most unlikely to achieve the target of cleaning of major rivers by 2007 and it
 may extend the target to XI Plan.  On this submission of the Ministry, the Committee express its serious concern on the
 tardy pace of execution of river cleaning project and recommends that all causative factors for the slow progress of the
 project be identified and sorted out expeditiously and all out efforts be made to accelerate the momentum required to
 achieve the stipulated targets within their scheduled time limit and cost estimates.Para 78)
Action Taken by the Ministry
            National River Conservation Plan is presently being implemented in 32 rivers spread over 19 States and 158 towns. 
 Planning Commission has allocated Rs.1417 crores as 10
th Plan outlay for the works under this Plan against the requirement
 of Rs.3066 crores for completion of these works.  A demand has already been placed with the Planning Commission to
 increase this outlay during the Mid-Term Review, which is still underway.  Unless these funds are made available, the
 Ministry is not in a position to complete the approved works and achieve the target of cleaning of major rivers by  2007. 
 also the present approved works do not cover full pollution load in the major rivers like Ganga, Yamuna etc. for which an
 additional Rs.3064 crores is required.  All these requirements have been given to the Planning Commission and are
 necessary to meet the objective of cleaning of major rivers by 2007.
            In spite of the meagre resources for completing the approved works, additional sewage treatment capacity of 375 mld
 (million litres per day) was created during 2004-05 under NRCP and a further sewage treatment capacity of 564 mld is
 expected to be added during the current financial year.  It is, therefore, evident that the execution of river cleaning schemes
 is progressing satisfactorily commensurate with the funds available in the Outlay.
            Further, all the Systemic issues associated with the river cleaning projects have been identified and a detailed review
 of the works is being undertaken at the highest level in the Ministry by Secretary (E&F).  Monitoring of progress of works
 is being strengthened and  process has been initiated for appointment of independent Evaluators for the works being done
 under NRCD.  Meetings of the Steering Committee of National River Conservation Authority are also being held to review
 the progress of works with different States and to accelerate the momentum of works to achieve the stipulated targets
 commensurate with the outlay within the scheduled time limit and cost estimates.
Comments
            The Committee is not at all pleased with the present situation as it has now been informed that due to non-availability
 of sufficient funds, the project of cleaning of rivers cannot be completed  by 2007, the target fixed for this purpose and is
 likely to be extended to the XI Plan period. This means the cost of the project will increase. The Committee fails to
 understand as to why the issue of funds was not sorted out at the time of fixing the target. The Committee would like to
 have the comments of the Planning Commission and the Ministry in this regard, particularly the reasons/constraints for non-
completion of the Project as per the target.
NATIONAL LAKE CONSERVATION PLAN (NLCP)
Recommendation
            The Committee feels that lakes are critical in sustaining the environmental health of our country.  Acting as a huge
 reservoir, they not only provide water but also recharge and replenish the ground water and prevent floods.  Besides, their
 importance from the point of view of beauty, and aesthetics are well acclaimed.  But the Committee is not satisfied with the
 lackadaisical approach of the Ministry in undertaking the lake conservation schemes.  They are moving without any specific
 targets and objectives.  The Committee is anguished to note that even after repeated recommendations of the Committee,
 the Ministry has not come out with any specific targets to be achieved during a particular period.  The Committee expresses
 its serious concern and recommends that the Government should formulate short-term and long-term plans on lake
 conservation with specific targets and should proceed further in that direction as per those targets.

Action Taken by the Ministry
The scheme of National Lake Conservation Plan(NLCP) was initiated in June, 2001 with the objective to restore and
 conserve polluted and degraded lakes of the country.  During the four year period since inception of NLCP, 20 projects for
 conservation of 35 lakes at an estimated cost of about Rs. 164 crore have been approved.  The activities covered under the
 programme include: Prevention of pollution from point sources by interception, diversion and treatment of pollution load
 entering the lake, insitu conservation measures like desilting, deweeding, bioremediation, biomanipulation, construction of
 wetland for nutrient development including lake beautification and public recreation facilities, public awareness and
 participation besides site specific activities.
The scheme of NLCP was conceptualized in 1994 and put up for approval of Government of India in Dec, 1997.  However,
 at that point of time, the Ministry was requested to seek external assistance for NLCP.  Since no funding agency evinced
 any interest, the scheme was later granted approval in June, 2001, after which its implementation  was initiated.  During the
 4 year period of implementation, the number of lakes taken up for conservation has gradually increased reaching 35 at
 present along with a progressive expenditure trend. With a view to prioritise the lakes for conservation under NLCP, the
 Ministry identified 62 lakes on the basis of a criteria.  The list of identified lakes have been communicated to all State
 Governments for amendments/ if any with justification.  Some of the States have indicated their prioritization of lakes.  A
 national prioritization list  shall be prepared after receipt of inputs from all the States.  The Ministry in the meantime has
 prepared short-term targets for the current financial year which include Physical completion of conservation works in 8
 lakes along with coverage of 3.66 Ha lake area through bioremediation resulting in improved dissolved oxygen content and
 reduction in organic matter with weed control.  Besides this, interception and diversion of sewage, realignment of drains,
 check dam, setting up of settling tanks, desilting & deweeding, catchment area treatment including afforestation along with
 public participation and public/private partnership are also proposed to be achieved in respect of a few lakes.
Comments
            The Committee is not satisfied with the action taken by the Ministry in conserving the lakes of the country.  It is
 constrained to say that a big project like NLCP, which could play a significant role in restoring the environmental health of
 the country, is suffering due to apathy and the lackadaisical attitude of the Central and State Governments.  Very little
 seems to have been done for cleaning of lakes and a lot of time has been consumed in preparing action plans or discussing
 cost factors.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the programme needs to be executed with all seriousness and
 commitment by the concerned parties.

FOUNDATION FOR REVITALIZATION OF LOCAL HEALTH TRADITIONS (FRLHT)
Recommendation
            The Committee is of the view that 90% of the country's medicinal plants occur in forest habitats.  The most important
 strategy for conserving the medicinal plant gene pools is to establish a nation wide network of forest gene banks (average
 size 200-500 ha in tropical forest and 50-100 ha in high altitude forest) across the different forest types and altitudinal range
 in all bio-geographic regions of the country.  In view thereof, the Committee recommends that Ministry should urgently
 initiate programmes or in-situ conservation of genetic diversity.  The Committee also feels that conservation of genetic
 diversity and documenting the entire traditional medicinal plants should be undertaken in such a manner so as to plan for
 development of traditional medicinal plants.  Besides, the Ministry, in collaboration with CSIR, DST, DBT and Ministry of
 Rural Development, should support community owned enterprises based on medicinal plants.            (Para 98)
Action Taken by the Ministry
India has an estimated 8000 species of native medicinal plants.  These are distributed across all vegetation types and
 altitudinal ranges across all the bio-geographic regions of the country.  Conservation of these species can therefore only be
 done by protecting a large number of forest areas, comprising 15 to 20 forest sites in every State, across all the bio-
geographic regions.  The forestry sector undertakes in-situ conservation of the medicinal plants diversity of the country. In
 situ conservation serves the purpose of long-term survival and evolution of a species in  association with other plant, animal
 & microbial associates in the ecosystem.
Since MOEF is now administering the Biodiversity Act 2002, it has an additional mandate of supporting the conservation of
 traditional knowledge associated with the use of medicinal plants biodiversity.
            At present a number of organizations and departments, viz., ICMR, CIMAP, DBT, NBPGR, and Ministry of
 Commerce are also engaged in handling the subject of medicinal plants but each one has a specific mandate.  While it is
 research for the first three organizations, it is ex-situ conservation for NBPGR, and marketing for the Ministry of
 Commerce.  Similarly, research on cultivation of medicinal plants, especially pertaining  to standardization of agro-
technology & breeding techniques is managed by the Ministry of Agriculture.  The Indian Medicinal Plant Board was
 established vide Gazette Notification dated 24.11.2000, following the recommendations of the Planning Commission’s Task
 Force.  The basic role of Indian Medicinal Plant Board has been that of coordination and advisory, and limited to promoting
 cultivation (contract farming), extension activities and market research through project mode.  
            Considering   the extent and magnitude of work involved in in-situ and ex-situ conservation of medicinal plants, and
 the need for more than one agency having to be pro-active player and having been also recognized in the Planning
 Commission Task Force report, the Ministry of Environment and Forests would like to reaffirm the validity and relevance
 of its seminal role in conservation of medicinal plant.  The concerns arising out of CITES and CBD also provide an added

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment
 and Forests, having been authorized by the Committee, present its 154
th Report relating to Wild Life (Protection)
 Amendment *Bill 2005.  The Bill seeks to amend the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.

REPORT
 
                        As per the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill, the Project Tiger was launched in the country on
 1st April, 1973 for conserving the endangered tiger.  Initially, 9 Tiger Reserves were covered under the project, which
 has now increased to 28 Tiger Reserves, falling in 17 States.  The Central Government provides funding support to
 projects prepared by the States in this regard.  Since then, the Project Tiger is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme.  The
 implementation of the project over the years highlighted the need for a statutory authority, having legal backing with
 well-defined functions, for conservation of tigers in the country.  Despite the project ongoing for more than three
 decades, the status of tigers in the country remains critical, which necessitates the need for addressing the issue right
 from planning to administration and making provisions for dealing with cases of violation.
                        Any conservation effort to save tiger, must take care of the prevailing peculiar circumstances in the
 country, where forests are not wilderness areas but also where tribal and other people live.  On the basis of the
 recommendations of the National Board for Wild Life, a Task Force  was setup to look into the problems of tiger
 conservation in the country and to suggest comprehensive measures for its improvement.
                        The recommendations of the Task Force, inter alia, include strengthening of Project Tiger by giving it
 statutory as well as administrative powers.  It has also recommended that the report relating to Project Tiger should
 annually be sent to the Central Government for laying in Parliament so that the commitment to the Project Tiger is
 reviewed from time to time.
                        With this twin objective of tiger conservation and harmonizing the rights of the tribal people living in and
 around tiger reserves, it is proposed to amend the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, to provide for the National Tiger
 Conservation Authority responsible for implementation of Project Tiger plan for protecting endangered tigers; and to
 harmonize and facilitate the implementation of the Tiger Conservation Plans prepared by the State Governments taking
 in to account the needs and concerns of the local people.  The amendments are aimed at putting in place, a mechanism
 which will balance and manage, the livelihood needs of the local people with the imperatives of tiger conservation.
                       
The salient features of the Bill are as under :
 
(i)         The Bill seeks to constitute a National Tiger Conservation Authorityto exercise the powers conferred on, and to
 perform the functions assigned to it under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.  The National Tiger Conservation
 Authority has been proposed under the Chairmanship of the Minister of Environment and Forests.
 
Preparation of Annual Report of the Tiger Conservation Authority and submission of the audit report to the Central
 Government for laying before Parliament.
 
State level Steering Committee has been proposed in the tiger states under the Chairmanship of respective Chief
 Ministers for ensuring co-ordination, monitoring, protection and conservation of tiger, co-predators and prey animals
 within the tiger range States.
(iv)       The State Government shall, on the recommendations of the National Tiger Conservation Authority, notify an
 area as a tiger reserve. The State Government shall prepare a Tiger Conservation Plan including staff development and
 deployment plan for the proper management of tiger reserve.
(v)        No alteration in the boundaries of tiger reserve shall be made except on a recommendation of the National Tiger
 Conservation Authority and the approval of the National Board for Wild Life. No State Government shall de-notify a
 tiger reserve, except in public interest with the approval of the Tiger Conservation Authority and the National Board for
 Wild Life.
(vi)       It has been proposed that the State Government shall establish a Tiger Conservation Foundation for tiger reserves
 within the State in order to facilitate and support their management for conservation of tiger and biodiversity and, to take
 initiatives in eco-development by involvement of people in such development process.
(vii)      Some other changes of consequential and incidental nature have also been proposed in the bill.

The Committee recommends insertion of the words ‘outside the core area’ after the words ‘tiger reserve’.
Clause 3
            V         Section 51(1) – New Proviso
The Committee sought certain clarifications on the adequacy of the penal provision proposed in Section 51 of the
 Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.  It has been informed that regarding higher punishment proposed to be provided to the
 person accused of offences, it is always made relatable to the nature of the offence committed and punishment is
 accordingly awarded commensurate with such offences.  For example, section 304 of the IPC makes provision for
 punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder and a punishment for life or up to ten years is provided. 
 Under section 307 for attempt to murder, the imprisonment may extend to ten years, whereas under section 304A,
 causing death by negligence, the imprisonment may extend to two years only.  Keeping all this in view, it seems that the
 punishment proposed in the Bill is in line with the punishment provided in the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972.  The
 Ministry of Environment & Forests, however, agreed with the views of the Committee that the amount of penalty could
 be increased keeping in view the value of the endangered tiger.
                                    The Committee, therefore, recommends that the following Sub-Sections may be inserted after Sub-
Section (1 B) of the Principal Act to make the offence more deterrent.
“(1C) – Any person, who commits an offence in relation to the core of a tiger reserve or where the offence relate to
 hunting in the tiger reserve or altering the boundaries of the tiger reserve, such offence shall be punishable on first
 conviction with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but may extend to seven years, and also
 with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two lakh rupees, and in the event of a
 second or subsequent conviction with imprisonment for a term  of not less than seven years and also with fine which
 shall not be less than five lakh rupees but may extend to fifty lakh rupees.
            (1D) – Whoever abets any offence punishable under sub-section (1C) shall, if the act abetted is committed in
 consequence of the abetment, be punishable with the punishment provided for that offence”.
 
VI        Clause 1, Enacting Formula and Title          
 
Clause 1, the enacting formula and the title are adopted with some consequential changes, which are of consequential or
 drafting nature, namely, the figure ‘2005’ and the words ‘Fifty-sixth’ to be substituted by the figure ’2006’ and the
 words ‘Fifty-seventh’, respectively.

The Committee recommends that the Bill may be passed after incorporating the amendments suggested by it.

 compensation to people for loss incurred on account of wild animals are concerned, the same would be provided in the

                        The protection of tigers has reached a very critical state and if the issue is not addressed effectively there

 bureau has to be set-up, it should work effectively on different level, one, to strengthen the enforcement at the state

 two-tiered approach: set-up a Wild Life Crime Bureau at the Central level, with nodes in each tiger range state in which

 immediate need to set up a Wild Life Crime Bureau as a statutory body under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 to
 make it effective and control the crime relating to wild life. It accordingly, recommends that this should be done on a
 priority basis at the earliest.

REPORT
Since time immemorial human civilization has progressed on twin wheels of Science and Technology and Trade. Right from the days of stone tools to
 the modern days of robotic assembly lines, societies which were technologically ahead not only gave better material conditions to it’s members but also heavily
 impacted on the value systems of the society, encouraging values like rationalism which, in-turn, paved way for further progress.     History is witness to the
 fact that science has fundamentally changed human civilizations.  Whether it was the stone age or the modern age of bio-technology and space exploration, man
 has been continually metamorphosing  his immediate environment to suit his needs of the day.  Science cannot be denied the credit for solving many of the
 human problems, if not all. 
2.         In ancient time India had strong tradition of scientific enquiry and rational analysis.  The world owes the zero and the decimal systems to India.  After

International S&T Co-operation
Support high quality research in autonomous bodies where specialization ranges from advanced medical research materials to astronomy.
Catalyzing S&T interaction in societal programmes, and entrepreneurship development
Science popularisation, communication and S&T Management Information System
Promotion of Commercialisation of home grown technology
Support to technology development programmes, technology information and assessment
Surveying & Mapping (Survey of India and National Atlas &  Thematic Mapping Organisation)
Meteorology (IMD)

Indian Association for Cultivation of Science, Kolkata
11.       The Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, Kolkata established in July 1876, is a national institution for higher learning whose primary
 purpose is to foster high quality fundamental research in frontier disciplines of the basic sciences. Founded by Dr. Mahendra Lal Sircar, a philanthropist, the
 activities at the Association in the very early years were supported by generous public contributions. It was conceived and planned in the backdrop of the great
 cultural and intellectual awakening of the nineteenth century Bengal and was desired by its founder to be an institution 'solely native and purely national'. The
 original objective of the Association, which continues even today, was to cultivate science in all its departments both with a view to its advancement by original
 research and to its varied applications to the arts and comforts of life.
12.       Now it is an autonomous body funded by the Department of Science and Technology (DST) of the government of India and by the government of West
 Bengal. A number of specific projects raised by individual scientists or groups of scientists are being supported by different funding agencies such as CSIR,
 DAE, DNES, DST, DOS, DSIR, ICMR, INSA, NSF, UGC and UNDP. The Institute has dynamic programmes for the pursuit of research leading to the doctoral
 degree and for post-doctoral work and has Visiting Scientists Scheme.

The Institute will conduct R&D in thrust areas of physical and chemical sciences including energy research for advancement of knowledge.
Continue programme on cancer biology and bioenergitics.
Physico-chemical studies of adsorption of textile dye on to microbial biomass.
Studies in porous materials using transition metals.
A new phase for the synthesis and charactorisation of oxides and sulfides with different aligned 1-D nanoforms and suitable dopanpants will be started to tailor
 their optical properties for photonic applications.

 Parliamentary Standing  Committee’s recommendation  in its 149
th Report which has recommended that the institutes like Indian Association for the

 replacement of obsolete equipment and also create state-of-the-art facilities for conducting research in frontier areas of science and technology like nano-
materials, ultra fast chemical reactions etc.

 for buying new instruments for its  better functioning.  The Committee suggests that the Department may take up the matter with the concerned State
 Government to acquire land for the said purpose.

49.       In a country where efforts have been made during the last fifty years to achieve total literacy, spreading scientific awareness, remove superstition and

 other side of the digital divide that is largely rural, backward, steeped in regressive social values and superstitious thinking. The challenge before the

National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF)
Objectives:
50.       The National Centre for  Medium Range Weather  Forecasting  is a mission  mode project of  the Government presently  functioning  as Division  of
 DST. Its  objectives  are development  of an NWP system for generating  location specific forecasts  for providing  weather based agro-advisory services  to
 farmers, and  NWP guidance  to other user agencies, including India Meteorological Department and Defence. It has three Divisions, viz: Research Divisions,
 which is responsible for development/implementation of models data assimilation system and diagnostics, Application Division which is responsible for
 coordinating  agro-met Advisory Services in 127 Agro-climatic zones, and for customizing  forecast products for different user agencies, and Computer
 Division responsible  for acquiring and maintaining  computer systems and infra-structure supports.  
Major Achievements during 2005-06 were:
51.       The major goal of the centre is to produce in real time the best possible weather forecasts for the country. NCMRWF implemented All India medium
 range weather forecast bulletin for media, web based district  level  forecast and increased the number  of Agro-Advisory Service Units (AAS) from 83 to 107
 during the year 2005-2006. All India weekly agro-advisory was prepared and disseminated to 400 users during  monsoon period of  2005. NCMRWF provided
 its medium range weather forecasts to various sectors like  energy  (Petroleum /Power), Transport , Water Resources, Adventure and sports and Defence. As a
 capacity building measure conducted a number of training programmes for different users like Navy, Airforce and AAS Unit personnel. The computing power
 at the Centre was enhanced form 28.8 Gflops to 486 Gfops with the augmentation of Param Padma machine. A 3-DVAR mesoscale data assimilation scheme
 was also implemented during the year 2005-2006.   This year computing power enhanced to 1.3 terrflop. by upgrading CRAY SVI to CRAY XI E.
Proposed Programmes for the year 2006-2007
52.       The efforts to upgrade computing and infrastructure facilities shall continue with a aim to become and remain internationally competitive. It is proposed
 to deploy Automatic Weather Station (AWS) in a phased manner at all the AAS units which shall enable NCMRWF to provided District level Agro-advisory
 Services. It is envisaged that computing power will increase to 1.2 Tflops in the year 2006-07 and this shall enable NCMRWF to run a 75 km resolution Global
 Model for improved forecast accuracy. WRF model shall be made operational at a 12 km resolution for Tropical Cyclone forecast. NCMRWF shall also run a
 16 member Ensemble prediction system to arrive at a statistically significant  forecast. The experimental extended range/ seasonal prediction system shall be
 made operational. Apart from the above, NCMRWF shall incorporate Radiance assimilation, contribute in various field campaigns like meso-Network.  It is
 expected that the Web-based Data service shall be operational and the BIMSTEC center shall be converted to real mode with full infrastructure.
53.       There is fluctuation in allocation for National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting from Rs. 22.00 crores in B.E.  2005-06 to Rs. 19.00 crores
 in R.E. of the same year.  In 2006-2007 allocation has been increased to Rs. 25.25 crores in B.E.  The Committee has been informed that the reduction in budget
 allocation of NCMRWF from Rs. 22.00 crores in B.E. 2005-2006 to Rs. 19 crores in RE 2005-2006 is due to saving in salary, foreign travel, supplies &
 material, office expenses and professional services.Allocation in BE 2006-07 is enhanced to Rs. 25.25 crores to upgrade  computing and infrastructure facilities,
 visualization, networking, I.T. infrastructure with emerging technology, etc. and to purchase equipments for auditorium.  The provisions, which are based on an
 assessment of requirements, may undergo changes based on actual progress of schemes which is dependent on several factors.  In case additional requirements
 arise during the course of the year, the provisions can be enhanced, based on needs at the RE stage.  Therefore, the budget provisions made at the BE stage do
 not adversely affect the programmes of the Centre.
54.       The Committee recommends that the upgradation of computing and infrastructure facilities, visualization, networking, I.T. infrastructure should be done
 as soon as possible. Since the objectives of the Centre is to generate  location specific forecasts  for providing  weather based agro-advisory services  to farmers,
 and  NWP guidance  to other user agencies, including India Meteorological Department and Defence, upgradation  of existing technologies is the need of the
 hour. Weather forecasting needs constant improvements both in technology as well as expertise. The Country still has substantial number of farmers caught in
 the vagaries of unpredictable monsoon and other natural phenomenon. They can  immensely benefit from better forecasting in the future.
TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT BOARD
55.       The Government of India constituted Technology Development Board(TDB) in September, 1996, under the provisions of the Technology Development
 Board Act, 1995, with adequate fund to consolidate further Technology Development in the country by bringing together the efforts of industry and R&D
 institutions for achieving integrated excellence. Therefore, the main objective of the Board is development and commercialisation of indigenous technology and
 adaptation of imported technology for wider domestic application. For the achievement of this objective, the Board provides financial assistance in the form of
 equity, loan and grant out of the fund administered by the Board to companies engaged in commercialisation of indigenous technology etc. Besides, TDB also
 endeavours to provide a framework that would facilitate and stimulate coming together of an entrepreneur and innovator to respond to market demand.
Major Achievements during 2005-06 were:
56.       During 2005-06, TDB has signed 18 agreements having project cost of Rs.223.40 crores against which TDB’s commitment is for Rs.69.69 crores and
 Rs.70.13 crores (including the disbursement of pending commitments of previous years) have so far been disbursed. 
57.       The distinction achieved in the treatment of distillery effluent, seed support for STEP/TDB’s, Drinking water purification based on membrane filtration
 technology, Polyherbal patented inventions, Power from municipal solid waste, Antigens and Proteins from native source, software medical diagnostic and
 Recombinant Human Platelet Deriver growth factor are worth special mention.
Proposed Programme for the year 2006-2007
58.       TDB will enhance its potential to provide financial assistance (loan, equity and grant) to promote development and commercialisation of indigenous
 technology and adoption of imported technology. The Board will also play an important role in priority support to Techno-entrepreneur In the end of 2005-06
 the Board will still have 59 proposals out of 110 received to be considered during next financial year. In order to meet the pending commitment and those of
 next financial year, TDB has made a provision of Rs.112 crores for the disbursement of loan and grant during the year 2006-07. It may be added that
 disbursement of loan, grant and equity is made out of the grant-in-aid received from DST and also from the internal source of TDB.

            Objectives
61.       The Scheme “Synergy Projects” has targeted to achieve the objectives of studies, pilot projects and development efforts that can nucleate or catalyze
 large multi-disciplinary projects or help in networking institutions whose work has a common objectives but the efforts are currently fragmented.  They are

 the projects undertaken by the Office of the Principal Scientific Advisor to GOI relate to improving S&T environment in the country. 
Major Achievements during 2005-06 were:
62.       Among projects, RuTAG, a Specialized Rural Technology Up-gradation Project has been initiated in the States of Tamilnadu, Uttaranchal, Karnataka
 and Rajasthan through various collaborative programmes with specialized institutions such as BARC, CFTRI, IGCAR, IITs and National Institutes of
 Technology  with the partnership of State Government and NGOs.  Based on the recommendations of Core group for R&D in the automotive sector (named
 CAR), six thrust areas were identified and expert panels were constituted to prepare status papers on each of these areas.   The proposals for projects like (a)
 Advanced Materials – Hyderforming and tailor welded blanks (b) Low cost engine management system for 2 or 3 wheelers  (c) Intelligent and interactive
 telematics using the wireless technologies for transportation systems and  (d) project on telematics for Traffic Control and Vehicle Tracking at Koyembedu Bus
 Terminus, Chennai are designed for development of technology in pre-competitive stage.  The projects on the development of a Bulk Encryption Unit and on
 the development of an explosive detector are scheduled to complete successfully in March, 2006.

63.       Besides the current projects Machine Tool Manufacturing Sector has been identified as key area of cooperation, collaborative research, development and
 technology support in a meeting organized at IISc, Bangalore on 8.10.2005 by a large number of industry representatives and faculty members of the
 institutions.    In the next step, specific proposals will be drawn up for collaborative programmes/projects to be taken up for technology development.  As it has
 been done in the automotive sector, these projects will also attempt to address issues through a consortium of industries and institutions in pre-competitive

 part of the next fiscal.  The implementing organizations would include the Semiconductor Complex Ltd., Punjab; The Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic
 Research, Kalpakkam; the Central Scientific Instruments Organisation, Chandigarh; the Terminal Ballistics Research Laboratory, Chandigarh and the Indian
 Institute of Technology, Bombay.

 by the Office of the Principal Scientific Advisor to the Government of India are coming up with pilot projects which can nucleate and calalyze major multi-
disciplinary projects or help in networking institutions, who have worked on a common objective but whose efforts are presently fragmented.  These projects
 relate to national development or national security.  The physical outputs that the Synergy Projects are aiming at to achieve are a national Energy Map for India
 i.e. MARKAL, analysis of Indian Patenting activity in the International and Domestic Patent System, evolution of high-tech technologies in critical areas of
 mission oriented agencies, evolution of materials scenario and performance in critical areas by mission oriented agencies, GaAS- Epitaxial multi junction
 Quantum Well Infrared Photo detectors (QWIPs), preparing test bed for QWIPs arrays explosive detectors based on IMS technology, identification of recharge

 of scarce resources. As these projects relate to national development or national security, they acquire much more importance. The Committee feels that
 formulation of National Energy Map, providing direction to face the challenges of emerging international patent regime and coordination of mission oriented
 projects should be under taken with the seriousness they deserve, as they will determine the emerging contours of  future development.

 about scientific development among the masses. This Channel can also help bringing masses to the fold of the mainstream and build their potential to
 participate in national development and get benefited by them.
